title: Long-lived Quantum Memories With Rare-earth Ions Doped In Crystals
authors: Yu-Yu Sa, Pei-Xi Liu, Zong-Quan Zhou, Chuan-Feng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum memory is a core enabling device for large-scale quantum networks, serving as the fundamental building block for quantum repeaters and transportable quantum memories. Among various physical platforms, rare-earth-ion-doped crystals stand out as one of the most promising solid-state candidates for long-lived photonic quantum memories, owing to their exceptionally long spin coherence time and their compatibility with integration. In this review, we first introduce the physical mechanisms underlying long-lived spin coherence in rare-earth systems, with particular emphasis on the zero-first-order-Zeeman transition and dynamical decoupling techniques. We then review the experimental progress in this field, highlighting three distinct lifetimes--the spin coherence time, the light storage time, and the quantum storage time--and covering experiments that have achieved hour-scale spin coherence, minute- to hour-scale light storage, and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges that hinder the realization of practical long-lived quantum memories, explore potential strategies to overcome these obstacles, and outline the prospects for their future applications in quantum networks.
tldr: This review surveys long-lived photonic quantum memories based on rare-earth-ion-doped crystals, focusing on spin coherence mechanisms and experimental progress toward quantum repeater applications.
motivation: Quantum memories are essential building blocks for large-scale quantum networks and quantum repeaters, and rare-earth-ion-doped crystals are promising solid-state platforms due to their long spin coherence times and integration compatibility.
method: The authors review the physical mechanisms enabling long-lived spin coherence, especially the zero-first-order-Zeeman transition and dynamical decoupling, and survey experimental milestones across spin coherence time, light storage time, and quantum storage time.
result: The review reports experiments achieving hour-scale spin coherence, minute- to hour-scale light storage, and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage, while identifying remaining challenges for practical long-lived memories.
conclusion: Rare-earth-ion-doped crystals are a leading platform for long-lived quantum memories, and overcoming the discussed obstacles could enable future quantum network and repeater applications.

title: Long-range Entangled Criticality From Coherent Errors
authors: Amir-Reza Negari, Subhayan Sahu, Jan Behrends, Benjamin B\'eri, Timothy H. Hsieh
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We find that coherent error can induce a phase transition from the clean surface code phase into an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length. To demonstrate this, we establish two general results of independent interest. The first relates topology and quantum information to mixed-state entanglement: we show that when a noise channel acting on a topological code preserves a higher-form symmetry and nonzero coherent information, the noisy state for generic logical input is long-range entangled. The second generalizes the local recovery construction based on finite Markov length to any locally parameterized family, thus encompassing local Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing, and thermal states. We apply these results to the honeycomb surface code, in which we find an extended long-range entangled critical regime that is a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. As a byproduct of these studies, we relate the conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model.
tldr: The paper shows that coherent errors can drive a topological code into an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length.
motivation: Understanding mixed-state entanglement and error-induced phases in topological codes is important for quantum information, especially when coherent errors break the standard clean surface-code picture.
method: The authors prove general results connecting higher-form symmetry and coherent information to long-range entanglement in noisy topological states, and generalize local recovery constructions beyond finite Markov length to locally parameterized families including Lindbladian evolution and coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing.
result: Applied to the honeycomb surface code, they identify an extended long-range entangled critical regime interpreted as a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking, and relate conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model.
conclusion: Coherent errors can produce robust long-range entangled criticality in topological codes, revealing new mixed-state entanglement phenomena and information-theoretic structure relevant to quantum error correction.

The authors establish two general results: first, that a noise channel preserving a higher-form symmetry and nonzero coherent information yields a long-range entangled state for generic logical inputs; second, that the local recovery construction based on finite Markov length generalizes to any locally parameterized family, including local Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors with syndrome dephasing, and thermal states. Applying these to the honeycomb surface code, they identify a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB). As a byproduct, they relate conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model.

title: Tight Quasiprobabilistic Entropic Uncertainty Relations For Discrete Quantum Systems
authors: Jonathan J. Thio, Stephan de Bi\`evre, Crispin H. W. Barnes, David R. M. Arvidsson-Shukur
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It was conjectured by Wehrl and proven by Lieb that the Shannon differential entropy of the Husimi function of a continuous-variable quantum state is lower bounded by the value it takes on coherent states. This corroborates the intuition, familiar from Heisenberg's uncertainty relations, that coherent states are minimal uncertainty states. The analogous statement for the Wigner function would be that the Wigner differential entropy of states with a positive Wigner function is bounded below by the entropy of pure Gaussian states. This was conjectured a decade ago, but recently disproven. Here, we prove the analogous statement for Kirkwood-Dirac distributions with mutually unbiased bases and for the Gross-Wigner distributions. For these discrete systems, the entropy-minimizing role is played by the pure states with positive quasiprobability distributions. Further, we prove that Kirkwood-Dirac distributions with large nonpositivity have large uncertainty.
tldr: The paper proves tight entropic uncertainty relations for discrete quantum systems using Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions with mutually unbiased bases and Gross-Wigner distributions.
motivation: Motivated by the Wehrl-Lieb conjecture for Husimi entropies and the recent disproof of the analogous Wigner-entropy conjecture, the authors seek discrete analogues that identify entropy-minimizing states and quantify uncertainty via quasiprobability nonpositivity.
method: They formulate entropic lower bounds for Kirkwood-Dirac distributions associated with mutually unbiased bases and for Gross-Wigner distributions, and relate large nonpositivity of Kirkwood-Dirac distributions to large uncertainty.
result: They show that pure states with positive quasiprobability distributions minimize the entropy for these discrete quasiprobabilistic distributions, and establish that strong nonpositivity implies strong entropic uncertainty.
conclusion: The work provides tight quasiprobabilistic entropic uncertainty relations for discrete quantum systems, extending continuous-variable entropy bounds to finite-dimensional settings and linking quasiprobability negativity to uncertainty.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper addresses entropy lower bounds for discrete quasiprobability distributions, specifically Kirkwood-Dirac (KD) distributions with mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) and Gross-Wigner distributions. Motivated by the Wehrl-Lieb theorem for the Husimi function and the recently disproven analogous conjecture for the Wigner function, the authors prove that for these discrete distributions, the Shannon entropy is minimized by pure states with positive quasiprobability distributions. They also establish a quantitative relationship between nonpositivity and uncertainty: KD distributions with large nonpositivity necessarily have large entropy. The work thus extends the program of characterizing minimal-uncertainty states via quasiprobability entropies to discrete settings where nonpositivity is intrinsic.

Establishes the analogous entropy lower bound for Gross-Wigner distributions, identifying pure states with positive quasiprobability distributions as entropy minimizers.
Demonstrates a quantitative trade-off: KD distributions with large nonpositivity imply large uncertainty, formalizing the intuition that nonclassicality costs in entropy.
Provides a discrete analogue of the Wehrl-Lieb conjecture in settings where the Wigner function conjecture fails, highlighting the role of positivity.

They analyze the Shannon entropy of discrete quasiprobability distributions, which can take negative values, and use the notion of nonpositivity (e.g., total negative volume) to quantify deviation from classicality. The proofs probably leverage the structure of MUBs and the Gross-Wigner formalism, possibly via majorization or uncertainty relations. The approach is analytical, with rigorous theorems and possibly small numerical illustrations (given the 5+4 page length).
deep_read.results_analysis: The main results are entropy lower bounds: for KD distributions with MUBs and for Gross-Wigner distributions, the minimal entropy is achieved by pure states with nonnegative quasiprobability distributions. This contrasts with the continuous-variable Wigner case, where the conjecture was disproven, suggesting that discreteness and the specific structure of MUBs/Gross-Wigner distributions restore the bound. Additionally, a quantitative relation between nonpositivity and entropy is proven, though specific constants or scaling are not detailed in the abstract. The results are theoretical and likely include inequalities of the form S(ρ) ≥ S(ρ_min) + f(nonpositivity), with f increasing.

Provides rigorous proofs for discrete settings, filling a gap in the literature and offering new insights into the role of positivity.

The practical implications for quantum computation or metrology are not explored; the results are foundational.
The abstract does not specify the exact form of the nonpositivity measure or the tightness of the bounds, which may limit immediate applicability.

It deals with quasiprobability distributions, uncertainty relations, and nonclassicality, which are core topics in quantum theory. Its novelty lies in the discrete focus and the quantitative nonpositivity-uncertainty trade-off. While concise, it is likely rigorous and impactful for the quantum foundations community, though its immediate practical relevance remains to be seen.

title: Decoy-state Quantum Key Distribution With A Leaky Mach-Zehnder Receiver
authors: Ryohei Mizusawa, \'alvaro Navarrete, Akihiro Mizutani, Kiyoshi Tamaki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the security of phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution for a Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and two threshold detectors that leak fine-grained information about the detection patterns. For this, we derive a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions and combine it with the decoy-state method and a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers. The leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, providing a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage even in the presence of beam-splitter imbalance. Our results provide a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers in the presence of receiver leakage.
tldr: The paper proves security for phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 QKD using a leaky Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and threshold detectors.
motivation: Practical QKD receivers can leak fine-grained detection information and have imperfect components, so security proofs must account for such imperfections in a loss-tolerant way.
method: The authors derive a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions, combine it with the decoy-state method, and apply a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers.
result: They obtain a leakage-induced phase-error rate correction that is independent of channel loss, enabling loss-tolerant security even with beam-splitter imbalance.
conclusion: The work provides a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers in the presence of receiver leakage.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a security proof for phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) using a Mach-Zehnder (MZ) receiver that is deliberately imperfect: the beam splitters are imbalanced and the two threshold detectors leak fine-grained information about detection patterns. The central technical problem is that real receivers deviate from the idealized loss-tolerant assumptions used in most security proofs, and detector leakage can correlate the adversary's side information with the detection outcome, potentially compromising the phase-error rate. The authors address this by deriving a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions (the probability that a single photon arrives and is detected in a way usable for key generation) for the imbalanced MZ receiver, then combining this bound with the standard decoy-state method to estimate single-photon yields and with a recent phase-error framework developed for leaky receivers. The key structural result is that the leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, which yields a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage even when beam-splitter imbalance is present. The paper is largely theoretical: it establishes composable security under stated assumptions and argues that the approach provides a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers. The abstract and extracted text do not report explicit numerical key-rate values, so the quantitative content is confined to the analytic bounds and the loss-independence property of the leakage correction.

Derives a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions for the imbalanced MZ receiver, making the single-photon analysis compatible with decoy-state estimation.
Combines the single-photon bound with the decoy-state method and a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers to bound the phase-error rate under leakage.

Establishes that the leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, giving a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage in the presence of beam-splitter imbalance.
Argues a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers with leakage, extending loss-tolerant methodology beyond idealized detector models.

The authors model the receiver explicitly: a Mach-Zehnder interferometer with imbalanced beam splitters and two threshold detectors, and they allow the detectors to leak fine-grained information about detection patterns to the adversary. The proof strategy has three coupled components. First, they compute a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contribution, i.e., the conditional probability that a single photon is routed and detected in a way that contributes to the sifted key, accounting for the imbalance of the beam splitters. Second, they apply the decoy-state method to estimate the relevant single-photon yield and error parameters from experimentally accessible intensities. Third, they invoke a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers to bound the phase-error rate, treating the leakage as side information available to Eve. The crucial technical step is showing that the leakage correction to the phase-error rate does not scale with channel loss, which is what makes the bound loss-tolerant. The analysis is composable in the sense that it aims to bound the full phase-error rate rather than only asymptotic quantities, though the extracted text does not detail the finite-key or composability parameters explicitly.

This is significant because loss-tolerant security proofs typically rely on the assumption that detection statistics are independent of loss in a controlled way; leakage can break that assumption, and showing the correction is loss-independent restores a loss-tolerant treatment. The paper also reports a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions for the imbalanced MZ receiver, which is the input needed for decoy-state estimation. However, the extracted text contains no explicit numerical key rates, no plots of secret-key rate versus distance or loss, and no quantitative comparison with prior leaky-receiver or imbalanced-receiver proofs. The four figures referenced in the metadata presumably contain such quantitative results, but they are not available in the extracted text. title: Optimised Finite Key For Satellite Up-link Entangled Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Thomas Jaeken, Faris Redza, Stefan B\"auml, Daniel K. L. Oi, Alessandro Fedrizzi, Jasminder S. Sidhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement-based quantum key distribution from ground to satellite has been proposed as a scalable primitive for global quantum networks and will be demonstrated as part of the imminent QEYSSat mission. Both theoretical studies and experimental emulations have shown that a significant asymptotic key rate can be expected. In this work we investigate this scenario with a more rigorous security analysis taking into account the finite size effects that arise from short block lengths common in satellite transmission. Our findings suggest a slight alteration of the optimal source operation when informed by finite statistics as opposed to the asymptotic regime, notably that the pump power should be slightly lowered. We quantify the annual key rate based on a dynamically optimised source operation for the Heriot-Watt ground station and several satellite parameters. We find an improved annual key rate when accumulating all raw key material before extracting a secure key instead of doing so for each overpass. We ultimately show that QEYSSat will be able to generate a significant secure annual key with both strategies.
tldr: This paper performs a finite-key security analysis for entanglement-based ground-to-satellite quantum key distribution and optimizes source operation for the QEYSSat mission.
motivation: Satellite-based entanglement QKD is a promising route to global quantum networks, but short overpass block lengths make asymptotic key-rate estimates insufficient for realistic mission planning.
method: The authors incorporate finite-size effects into the security analysis, dynamically optimize the source pump power, and quantify annual key rates for the Heriot-Watt ground station under several satellite parameters.
result: Finite-key statistics suggest slightly lowering the pump power compared with the asymptotic optimum, and accumulating raw key across overpasses before extraction improves the annual secure key rate.
conclusion: QEYSSat should be able to generate a significant annual secure key using either per-overpass or accumulated extraction strategies when source operation is optimized for finite-key conditions.

title: Gaussian Quantum Integrated Sensing And Communication
authors: Tuna Erdo\u{g}an, Shi-Yuan Wang, Shang-Jen Su, Matthieu R. Bloch
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a quantum integrated sensing and communication problem over an optical link in which a low-power transmitter simultaneously communicates with a receiver and identifies the range of a defect producing a backscattered signal. We model the system as a lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel, in which the target, modeled as a beamsplitter, affects the timing of the backscattered signal through its location. Motivated by the envisioned deployment of entanglement-enabled quantum networks, we develop two protocols that allow the transmitter to leverage shared Gaussian entanglement, in the form of independent two-mode squeezed vacuum states or coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum states, to assist both sensing and communication. Since entanglement is known to enhance sensing, as demonstrated in quantum illumination, and to increase communication rates through entanglement-assisted communication, the transmitter faces a trade-off in allocating its entanglement resources between the two tasks. Our main results characterize these trade-offs under the proposed protocols in terms of achievable communication rate/sensing error-exponent regions, which outperform time-sharing schemes and demonstrate a quantum advantage.
tldr: The paper analyzes entanglement-assisted Gaussian protocols for simultaneously communicating over and sensing a lossy thermal-noise bosonic optical link, characterizing achievable rate–sensing-error trade-offs.
motivation: Entanglement can enhance both quantum sensing, as in quantum illumination, and communication rates, but allocating shared entanglement between these tasks creates a fundamental trade-off.
method: The system is modeled as a lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel with a beamsplitter target affecting backscattered-signal timing; two protocols use independent two-mode squeezed vacuum or coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum states, and achievable communication-rate/sensing-error-exponent regions are derived.
result: The proposed protocols outperform time-sharing schemes and demonstrate a quantum advantage in the joint sensing-and-communication task.
conclusion: The work quantifies entanglement-resource trade-offs for integrated quantum sensing and communication and supports entanglement-enabled quantum network applications.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses a quantum integrated sensing and communication (QISAC) problem over an optical link, where a low-power transmitter simultaneously communicates with a receiver and estimates the range of a defect that produces a backscattered signal. The system is modeled as a lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel, with the target acting as a beamsplitter whose location determines the timing of the backscattered signal. Motivated by entanglement-enabled quantum networks, the authors propose two protocols that leverage shared Gaussian entanglement: one using independent two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) states and another using coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum (3MSV) states. The transmitter must allocate its entanglement resources between sensing and communication, creating a trade-off because entanglement enhances both quantum illumination (sensing) and entanglement-assisted communication rates. The main results characterize achievable communication rate versus sensing error-exponent regions for both protocols, showing that they outperform time-sharing schemes and demonstrate a quantum advantage. title: A Conditional Quantum Kac-Bernstein Theorem
authors: Hesam Hosseini, Jinpei Zhao, Masahito Hayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a conditional quantum Kac-Bernstein theorem for mixing of two independent, finite-mode bosonic inputs with quantum memories. We characterize exactly when the outputs are conditionally independent given both memories. Each input then decomposes into orthogonal memory sectors sharing a common Gaussian state on the physical system and a bosonic memory factor, up to sector-dependent physical displacements. In particular, triviality of the common bosonic factor implies separability of the inputs, as occurs whenever either memory has finite-dimensional support.
tldr: The paper proves a conditional quantum Kac-Bernstein theorem characterizing when mixed bosonic inputs with quantum memories become conditionally independent, with implications for separability.
motivation: The classical Kac-Bernstein theorem concerns independence and conditional independence under mixing; this work develops a quantum analogue for finite-mode bosonic systems with memory, aiming to understand the structure and separability of such states.
method: The authors analyze two independent bosonic inputs mixed via quantum memories and derive an exact decomposition of the inputs into orthogonal memory sectors, each sharing a common Gaussian state on the physical system plus a bosonic memory factor, up to sector-dependent displacements.
result: They obtain a complete characterization of conditional independence given both memories. In particular, triviality of the common bosonic factor implies separability of the inputs, which always occurs when either memory has finite-dimensional support.
conclusion: The theorem provides a structural link between conditional independence, Gaussian decompositions, and separability in bosonic systems with quantum memories, extending Kac-Bernstein-type results to the quantum regime.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper establishes a conditional quantum Kac-Bernstein theorem for the mixing of two independent, finite-mode bosonic inputs with quantum memories. The central result characterizes exactly when the outputs of a bosonic channel (or mixing process) are conditionally independent given both quantum memories. The authors prove that conditional independence implies a rigid structure: each input decomposes into orthogonal memory sectors that share a common Gaussian state on the physical (bosonic) system, multiplied by a bosonic memory factor, up to sector-dependent physical displacements. This extends the classical Kac-Bernstein theorem, which states that two independent random variables become conditionally independent given their sum only if they are Gaussian, to the quantum setting with memories. A key corollary is that if the common bosonic factor is trivial (e.g., the vacuum state), then the inputs are separable, and this occurs whenever either memory has finite-dimensional support. The work thus provides a precise algebraic and statistical characterization of when mixing of bosonic quantum states yields conditional independence, with implications for quantum information theory and the foundations of quantum probability.

title: Non-Hermitian Effective Dynamics From Post-selection Protocols
authors: Volker Meden Apostolos Siskou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiple seemingly distinct frameworks are commonly proposed to explain the emergence of effective non-Hermitian dynamics in quantum systems coupled to an environment. Furthermore, it remains contested how to properly calculate expectation values or whether thermal equilibrium states exist in non-Hermitian systems. In this work, we show that Feshbach projection, the Lindblad master equation, and the ancilla approach can all be understood through the Kraus map formalism, leading to non-Hermitian time evolution if an appropriate post-selection procedure is enforced. After first deriving an exact expression for the conditional system dynamics, we discuss the approximations employed in each approach and the classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that can be obtained. Within this framework, we physically justify the consistency of the right-right formalism (as opposed to the biorthogonal one) for calculating expectation values. Finally, we demonstrate that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium is not applicable to general non-Hermitian systems. Consequently, stationary states are characterized as non-equilibrium steady states, which should not be conflated with system-projected thermal states of the system-environment composite.
tldr: The paper unifies several frameworks for non-Hermitian effective dynamics via Kraus maps with post-selection and clarifies expectation values and equilibrium in such systems.
motivation: Multiple approaches to non-Hermitian dynamics in open quantum systems remain disconnected, and it is contested how to compute expectation values and whether thermal equilibrium states exist.
method: The authors derive exact conditional system dynamics using the Kraus map formalism under post-selection, then compare Feshbach projection, Lindblad master equation, and ancilla approaches along with their approximations and resulting non-Hermitian Hamiltonians.
result: They physically justify the right-right formalism for expectation values and show that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium does not apply to general non-Hermitian systems.
conclusion: Stationary states of general non-Hermitian systems should be characterized as non-equilibrium steady states rather than system-projected thermal states of the composite system-environment.

The central thesis is that all three frameworks can be unified under the Kraus map formalism, provided that a post-selection procedure is enforced on the environment. The authors first derive an exact expression for the conditional (post-selected) system dynamics, then systematically catalog the approximations each approach implicitly makes and the resulting classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians that can be generated. This unification is used to argue that the right-right formalism for expectation values is physically consistent, in contrast to the biorthogonal formalism, because it follows naturally from the conditional Kraus-map structure. Finally, the authors argue that the traditional notion of thermodynamic equilibrium does not apply to general non-Hermitian systems; stationary states should instead be characterized as non-equilibrium steady states, and these must not be conflated with system-projected thermal states of the composite system-environment. The paper is primarily conceptual and structural rather than numerical, aiming to resolve interpretive disputes by exposing a common mathematical backbone.

Derives an exact expression for the conditional system dynamics before approximation, providing a clean baseline against which each framework's approximations can be assessed.
Classifies the approximations employed in each approach and the corresponding classes of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians obtainable, clarifying the domain of validity of each method.
Provides a physical justification for the right-right formalism over the biorthogonal formalism for computing expectation values in non-Hermitian systems.

Argues that thermodynamic equilibrium is generally inapplicable to non-Hermitian systems, recharacterizing stationary states as non-equilibrium steady states distinct from projected thermal states of the composite.

The authors adopt the Kraus (operator-sum) representation of completely positive trace-preserving maps as the common language, then impose a post-selection condition on the environment to obtain conditional, non-trace-preserving system dynamics that can be recast as effective non-Hermitian evolution. By deriving the exact conditional map first, they create a reference point from which the Feshbach projection, Lindblad, and ancilla constructions are recovered as special cases under stated approximations (e.g., Markovianity, weak coupling, specific spectral or projection choices). This 'derive-exact-then-approximate' strategy is well suited to the paper's comparative goal, since it isolates precisely which step in each framework introduces the non-Hermiticity and which physical assumptions are smuggled in. The treatment of expectation values and thermodynamics is interpretive, building on the conditional-map structure to adjudicate between formalisms rather than testing against experiment.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper's results are structural rather than quantitative; no numerical values or experimental data are reported in the extracted text. A second result is the argument that the right-right formalism is the physically consistent choice for expectation values because it follows from the conditional probability structure of the post-selected map, whereas the biorthogonal formalism lacks this direct probabilistic interpretation. title: Unital Qubit Channels Are $3$-noisy
authors: Indu Bala, Preeti Parashar, Swapan Rana
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The algebraic and environmental characteristics of mixed unitary quantum operations are investigated. It is established that the composition of two uniformly n-mixed unitary channels is itself n-noisy, and this n-noisy property is shown to be an invariant under unitary equivalence. Furthermore, by utilizing majorization and the divisibility of Kraus rank-four unital qubit channels, we demonstrate that any unital qubit channel can be physically simulated using a three-dimensional maximally mixed environment. Together, these results advance the classification and physical realization of noisy quantum channels.
tldr: The paper proves that any unital qubit channel can be simulated with a three-dimensional maximally mixed environment and that the n-noisy property is preserved under composition and unitary equivalence.
motivation: The work aims to characterize mixed unitary quantum operations and clarify when noisy quantum channels admit simple physical realizations using small environments.
method: It combines algebraic arguments about uniformly n-mixed unitary channels with majorization techniques and the divisibility of Kraus rank-four unital qubit channels.
result: The authors show that compositions of uniformly n-mixed unitary channels remain n-noisy, that n-noisiness is unitarily invariant, and that every unital qubit channel is 3-noisy.
conclusion: These results advance the classification of noisy quantum channels and provide a minimal-environment physical simulation for unital qubit channels.

Second, using majorization and the divisibility of Kraus rank-four unital qubit channels, it shows that any unital qubit channel can be physically simulated using a three-dimensional maximally mixed environment. title: Anti-distinguishability Of Quantum Channels
authors: Nidhin Sudarsanan Ragini Ardra Ajitha Vijayan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study single-query perfect anti-distinguishability/exclusion tasks of finite quantum channel ensembles, primarily using associated Choi operators and process POVMs. Weak perfect anti-distinguishability requires each measurement outcome to exclude an ensemble candidate with certainty, whereas the strong form additionally requires every candidate to have an exclusion outcome occurring with non-zero probability. For pairs of channels, both coincide with perfect distinguishability, whereas larger ensembles exhibit separations. We derive Choi-operator-support-based obstructions: weak exclusion requires at least two rank-deficient Choi operators, while strong exclusion requires the support of every candidate Choi operator to be strictly contained in the joint Choi support. The common Choi support must also lie in the kernel of the PPOVM normalisation. For commuting Choi operators, this condition is sufficient for weak exclusion when the normalisation also commutes with them. Conversely, a nonzero admixture of the same noise channel into every candidate precludes weak exclusion for any probe. We apply these results to measure-and-prepare, state-space contraction, Pauli, and replacer channels. In particular, the full permutation-channel ensemble of an unlabeled POVM is strongly anti-distinguishable exactly when some POVM effect is rank-deficient, while replacer-channel exclusion reduces to state exclusion. A Choi-commuting ensemble exhibits strong exclusion with an unassisted probe although no positive-definite PPOVM normalisation permits even weak exclusion. In contrast, commuting qubit phase gates, whose Choi operators need not commute, admit exact convex-hull criteria for weak and strong exclusion, both attainable without assistance.
tldr: The paper develops theoretical criteria for perfect anti-distinguishability and exclusion of finite ensembles of quantum channels using Choi operators and process POVMs.
motivation: Quantum channel discrimination and exclusion are fundamental information-processing tasks, but exact anti-distinguishability conditions for channel ensembles are less understood than for states.
method: The authors formulate weak and strong perfect anti-distinguishability of channels via process POVMs and derive necessary and sufficient conditions based on supports and commutation properties of Choi operators.
result: They obtain Choi-support obstructions, characterize commuting and phase-gate ensembles, and apply the framework to measure-and-prepare, Pauli, contraction, permutation, and replacer channels.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic Choi-operator approach to channel exclusion and reveals separations between weak and strong anti-distinguishability for channel ensembles.

The authors define two notions: weak perfect anti-distinguishability, where each measurement outcome must exclude at least one ensemble candidate with certainty, and strong perfect anti-distinguishability, which additionally requires that every candidate has an exclusion outcome with non-zero probability. For pairs of channels, both notions coincide with perfect distinguishability, but for larger ensembles they can differ. The main technical tool is the support of Choi operators: weak exclusion requires at least two rank-deficient Choi operators, while strong exclusion requires that the support of every candidate's Choi operator be strictly contained in the joint Choi support. Furthermore, the common Choi support must lie in the kernel of the PPOVM normalization operator. For commuting Choi operators, this condition is also sufficient for weak exclusion when the normalization commutes with them. The authors show that a nonzero admixture of the same noise channel into every candidate precludes weak exclusion for any probe. They apply these results to several classes of channels: measure-and-prepare, state-space contraction, Pauli, and replacer channels. Notably, the full permutation-channel ensemble of an unlabeled POVM is strongly anti-distinguishable exactly when some POVM effect is rank-deficient, and replacer-channel exclusion reduces to state exclusion. They also present a Choi-commuting ensemble that exhibits strong exclusion with an unassisted probe, even though no positive-definite PPOVM normalization permits even weak exclusion. In contrast, commuting qubit phase gates, whose Choi operators need not commute, admit exact convex-hull criteria for weak and strong exclusion, both attainable without assistance.

The authors define weak and strong anti-distinguishability in terms of the existence of PPOVM elements that exclude candidates with certainty. They derive necessary conditions based on the rank deficiency of Choi operators and the containment of supports. title: Quantum Identity Authentication Protocol Via Perturbed Probability Amplitudes
authors: Xiangqun Fu, Zheng Han, Hongwei Li, Chun Zhou, Shuo Zhang, Jianhong Shi, Tan Li, Wansu Bao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum identity authentication is an effective solution for establishing mutual trust between communicating parties in the post-quantum era. To address the risk of partial secret information leakage under special measurements, this paper designs a quantum identity authentication protocol based on perturbed probability amplitudes. The protocol first proposes a method of encoding a random sequence onto the probability amplitudes of quantum entangled states, forming perturbed probability amplitudes, thereby reducing the involvement of shared information between the sender and receiver. Furthermore, it presents a method for generating n-bit random authentication information based on the n-bit pre-shared information, enhancing the randomness of the authentication information relative to an attacker. The proposed protocol can resist impersonation attack, CNOT attack, and entanglement measurement attack, and ensures backward security. title: Motional Decoherence Of The Internal State Of An Atom By Vacuum And Thermal Fluctuations Of A Quantum Field: Necessity Of A Fully Relativistic Treatment
authors: Bei-Lok Hu Jen-Tsung Hsiang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a massive object, such as a neutral atom or an Unruh-DeWitt detector, moving at constant speed in a quantum field and investigate how motion affects the quantum coherence of its internal degrees of freedom, manifesting as quantum dispersion in the absence of a quantum field, and decoherence in its presence. Our investigation aims to serve two purposes: One is to obtain the correct results for these effects, which are essential for the design of quantum information processing schemes where the quantum coherence of an atom's internal degrees of freedom is of major concern. The other is to expose the fallacies in commonplace approaches, which start with a non-relativistic calculation and then add on relativistic ``corrections". We first show a fully relativistic calculation of the internal dynamics based on covariance principles, and then one which ignores these principles, often justified by the atom's slow motion. By a direct comparison of results from these two approaches, we identify {significant discrepancies} in a non-relativistic treatment, even at low atomic speeds. The proper procedure, and a much safer one in terms of accuracy, is recommended here: first derive the dynamics and the necessary regularizations within a fully covariant relativistic framework. Only after the exact, internally consistent equations of motion are established should low-velocity limits be extracted from them. Only in this way can all the relativistic effects which matter: time dilation, aberration, non-inertial mass shifts, be systematically preserved, and accurate results obtained.
tldr: The paper shows that motional decoherence of an atom's internal state in a quantum field requires a fully relativistic covariant treatment, as non-relativistic approaches with perturbative corrections miss significant effects even at low speeds.
motivation: Accurate modeling of decoherence is essential for quantum information processing schemes that rely on the coherence of an atom's internal degrees of freedom, and commonplace non-relativistic calculations may be inadequate.
method: The authors perform a fully relativistic covariant calculation of the internal dynamics of a uniformly moving atom or Unruh-DeWitt detector coupled to vacuum and thermal quantum field fluctuations, and compare it directly with a non-relativistic treatment.
result: Significant discrepancies are found between the two approaches even at low atomic speeds, with relativistic effects such as time dilation, aberration, and non-inertial mass shifts playing an important role.
conclusion: The proper procedure is to first derive exact, internally consistent relativistic equations of motion and regularizations, and only then take low-velocity limits, in order to preserve all relevant relativistic effects and obtain accurate results.

The authors argue that the latter, common in the literature, leads to significant errors even at low speeds because it mishandles time dilation, aberration, and non-inertial mass shifts. They derive the exact relativistic equations of motion, including necessary regularizations, and then take the low-velocity limit to show discrepancies. The paper aims to correct results for quantum dispersion (in vacuum) and decoherence (in a field) and to advocate for a covariant-first methodology in quantum information schemes involving atomic coherence.

title: Entanglement Allocation For Quantum Integrated Sensing And Communication
authors: Shiva Kazemi Taskooh, Mehdi Monemi, Ekram Hossain, Georges Kaddoum, Mehdi Rasti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jointly supporting communication and distributed sensing over a shared, limited pool of entanglement resources is an attractive prospect for future quantum networks. We develop a network-level quantum integrated sensing and communication (Q-ISAC) framework in which a quantum base station dynamically allocates elementary Bell pairs between communication users and distributed sensing. Sensing resources are adaptively partitioned among multiple GHZ probes with dynamically selected sizes and sensing-node assignments. We derive an effective quantum Fisher information model accounting for probabilistic fusion, transmission loss, and memory decoherence, and formulate a finite-horizon allocation problem subject to communication QoS, expected sensing-information, sensing-reliability, and hardware constraints. A hierarchical constrained proximal policy optimization (HC-PPO) framework combines learned discrete sensing allocation with analytical continuous communication allocation. Numerical results show that GHZ probing requires approximately [MATH]--30% fewer sensing qubits than separable probing under modest probe-size caps and 65-67% fewer at the highest considered target under the same sensing requirements. Adaptive multi-GHZ partitioning provides greater robustness than single-GHZ sensing, while adaptive communication--sensing sharing outperforms the evaluated fixed splits. The proposed HC-PPO framework satisfies the joint requirements in at least 99.9% of test instances across the considered sensing targets and fusion probabilities. Monte Carlo evaluation separately shows that realized terminal information reached its target in 96-98% of realizations, distinguishing expected-information satisfaction from realized sensing performance.
tldr: The paper proposes a network-level quantum integrated sensing and communication framework that dynamically allocates shared Bell pairs between communication users and distributed GHZ-based sensing.
motivation: Future quantum networks will need to share limited entanglement resources between communication and distributed sensing tasks, motivating adaptive resource allocation rather than fixed splits.
method: It derives an effective quantum Fisher information model including probabilistic fusion, transmission loss, and memory decoherence, then formulates a finite-horizon constrained allocation problem solved by hierarchical constrained proximal policy optimization.
result: Numerical results show GHZ probing can require roughly 20–30% fewer sensing qubits than separable probing under modest caps and 65–67% fewer at the highest target, while the HC-PPO framework meets joint requirements in at least 99.9% of test instances.
conclusion: Adaptive entanglement allocation and multi-GHZ partitioning can improve qubit efficiency and robustness for joint quantum sensing and communication in future quantum networks.

title: An Example Of Universal Braiding In Links--Gould Topological Quantum Computation
authors: Ben-Michael Kohli Matthew Harper
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a universal quantum computational encoding via braiding in Links--Gould fusion spaces associated to [MATH] where [MATH] is on the unit circle and is not a root of unity. The calculations use explicit inclusions, projections, and Hermitian pairings without requiring [MATH]-matrices.
tldr: The paper constructs a universal quantum computing scheme via braiding in Links–Gould fusion spaces using neglectons, proving dense single-qubit gates and approximate arbitrary multi-qubit unitaries with small leakage.
motivation: Topological quantum computation seeks naturally fault-tolerant quantum gates from braiding non-Abelian excitations; this work explores Links–Gould fusion spaces as a route to universal braiding-based computation.
method: The authors use explicit morphism-space inclusions, projections, and Hermitian pairings under positivity and arithmetic constraints to define a finite-dimensional computational subspace without relying on R-matrices.

conclusion: Links–Gould fusion spaces provide a viable algebraic setting for universal topological quantum computation, with explicit control over leakage and Hermitian structure.

title: Universal Free-Electron-Sideband Control
authors: Tong Shen, Zhexin Zhao, Meng Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in free-electron quantum optics are establishing free electrons as a versatile quantum resource. Photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) interactions and free drift provide elementary operations for shaping the longitudinal electron wavefunction, yet their full control capabilities remain unexplored. Here, we prove that a finite sequence of alternating monochromatic PINEM interactions and free drifts can approximate any prescribed inner-product-preserving map from a finite-dimensional input subspace into the full ideal electron-sideband Hilbert space to arbitrary accuracy. We therefore call the protocol PINEMAD (PINEM And Drift). This framework encompasses state preparation, unitary gates, and isometric encoding. We further show numerically that parameter optimization enables high-fidelity state preparation at finite electron energy spreads, using experimentally accessible coupling strengths and tabletop-scale total drift lengths. These results establish electron energy sidebands as a programmable quantum resource.
tldr: The paper proves that alternating PINEM interactions and free drifts can approximate arbitrary inner-product-preserving maps on electron sidebands, enabling universal quantum control of free-electron states.
motivation: Free-electron quantum optics is emerging as a versatile quantum platform, but full control of the longitudinal electron wavefunction via PINEM and free drift has remained underexplored.
method: The authors introduce PINEMAD, a sequence of monochromatic PINEM interactions and free drifts, and prove universal approximation of isometric maps; they also numerically optimize parameters for finite electron energy spreads.
result: PINEMAD can approximate any prescribed isometric encoding from a finite-dimensional subspace into the electron-sideband Hilbert space, and numerical optimization achieves high-fidelity state preparation with experimentally accessible coupling strengths and tabletop drift lengths.
conclusion: Electron energy sidebands constitute a programmable quantum resource for state preparation, unitary gates, and isometric encoding, extending hybrid quantum control to free-electron platforms.

title: Information-Geometric Representation Of Upper Bounds On Fluctuation Growth In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Paul M. Alsing Newshaw Bahreyni
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on our earlier results for closed quantum systems, we investigate the dynamical evolution of quantum fluctuations and their connections to Fisher information and the quantum operations describing open-system dynamics. Starting from a general expression for the time derivative of an observable's uncertainty, we derive an alternative upper bound on fluctuation growth in an open quantum system using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The resulting bound separates contributions from the evolution of the quantum state and the explicit time dependence of the observable, reducing to a known result for closed-system dynamics. We then establish a connection between fluctuation dynamics and quantum Fisher information by decomposing the density operator and the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) into coherent and incoherent contributions, which leads to a bound relating the evolution of observable uncertainty to the coherent and incoherent components of the Fisher information, providing an information-geometric interpretation of fluctuation growth. To connect fluctuation dynamics with quantum operations governing open-system evolutions, we derive the time evolution of the eigenvalues of the density operator in terms of Kraus operators. Using the infinitesimal-time relation between Kraus and Lindblad operators, we obtain a corresponding expression for the eigenvalue dynamics in terms of Lindblad operators. This formulation directly relates changes in the density operator eigenvalues to the quantum processes acting on the system. We then study the results using some examples. Our results provide a framework connecting observable fluctuation growth, Fisher information, and the Kraus and Lindblad descriptions of quantum evolution, offering a route toward understanding how specific quantum channels influence the information and fluctuations available in an evolving quantum system.

title: Wavefront Engineering With Atomic Huygens' Surfaces Made Simple
authors: J. Ruostekoski K. E. Ballantine
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atomic arrays provide a cooperative platform for light-mediated interactions in nonlocal metasurfaces which can operate in the quantum regime without nanofabricated optical elements or intrinsic material absorption. We present a minimal atomic implementation to harness wavefront engineering and create a near-ideal intrinsic atomic Huygens' surface. A simple bilayer square lattice with a two-atom unit cell, not limited to small lattice spacings, provides near-unity reflectionless transmission and a full [MATH] phase control of transmitted light without the localized site-dependent level shifts of previous proposals. This simplification is achieved through nonlocal radiative excitations that provide the familiar electric-dipole response with even radiation parity as well as an odd-parity radiation channel whose leading multipolar interpretation combines magnetic-dipole and electric-quadrupole contributions in atoms exhibiting only electric dipole transitions. This eliminates the need to simultaneously excite pure electric-dipole and magnetic-dipole responses with exactly matched radiation. We derive a two-mode model for this response and show that it accurately captures full coupled-dipole simulations near the optimal lattice spacings. Because of the wide applicability of coupled-dipole models, the relevance of our microscopic analysis extends beyond atomic physics to nanostructured metasurfaces. Moreover, the same platform also connects directly to established subradiance-protected single-photon storage protocols, suggesting a route toward combining wavefront engineering, storage, and retrieval in a simple atomic bilayer.

title: Hardware-Efficient Reinforcement-Learned Scheduling For Quantum Ldpc Decoders
authors: Mohsen Moradi, Vahid Nourozi, Wei Tang, David Mitchell
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but their decoding algorithms present significant hardware implementation challenges. Reinforcement-learned sequential belief propagation (RL-S) improves the error-correction performance of conventional belief propagation (BP) through adaptive variable-node scheduling. However, its heap-based priority management introduces substantial hardware overhead. This paper presents hardware implementations of BP, RL-S, and bucket-based reinforcement-learned BP (BRL-S) for the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle QLDPC code. The BRL-S architectures employ quantized priorities and first-in, first-out (FIFO) buckets to simplify scheduling. Three configurations with two, four, and eight priority levels are evaluated. FPGA synthesis results demonstrate that BRL-S reduces lookup-table utilization by approximately 68--72% compared with RL-S. ASIC synthesis further shows reductions of 63--67% in area and 64--69% in estimated power consumption. These results demonstrate that bucket-based scheduling substantially improves the hardware efficiency of reinforcement-learned QLDPC decoders.
tldr: This paper presents hardware-efficient FPGA/ASIC implementations of reinforcement-learned scheduling for quantum LDPC decoders using bucket-based priorities.
motivation: QLDPC codes are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but their decoding algorithms face hardware implementation overhead, especially reinforcement-learned sequential belief propagation with heap-based scheduling.
method: The authors implement BP, RL-S, and bucket-based BRL-S decoders for the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle QLDPC code, using quantized priorities and FIFO buckets with two, four, and eight priority levels.
result: FPGA synthesis shows BRL-S reduces lookup-table utilization by about 68–72% versus RL-S, while ASIC synthesis shows 63–67% area reduction and 64–69% lower estimated power.
conclusion: Bucket-based scheduling substantially improves hardware efficiency of reinforcement-learned QLDPC decoders, making them more practical for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the hardware implementation challenges of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes, which are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The authors focus on the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle QLDPC code and compare three decoders: conventional belief propagation (BP), reinforcement-learned sequential BP (RL-S), and a novel bucket-based reinforcement-learned BP (BRL-S). RL-S improves error-correction performance by adaptively scheduling variable nodes using a heap-based priority queue, but this introduces significant hardware overhead. The proposed BRL-S replaces the heap with quantized priorities and first-in, first-out (FIFO) buckets, simplifying scheduling. Three BRL-S configurations with 2, 4, and 8 priority levels are evaluated. FPGA synthesis shows BRL-S reduces lookup-table (LUT) utilization by approximately 68–72% compared to RL-S. ASIC synthesis further demonstrates reductions of 63–67% in area and 64–69% in estimated power consumption. The results indicate that bucket-based scheduling substantially improves hardware efficiency while maintaining error-correction performance, making RL-based QLDPC decoders more practical for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

RL-S uses a heap-based priority queue to manage the scheduling order, which is hardware-expensive due to dynamic memory and complex control logic. The proposed BRL-S simplifies this by quantizing the priority values into a small number of levels (2, 4, or 8) and using FIFO buckets for each level. This approach reduces the need for a heap and enables a simpler hardware architecture. The authors implement BP, RL-S, and BRL-S decoders for the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle QLDPC code, likely using a fixed-point representation. title: On The (Quantum) Communication Complexity Of Secure Mpc From A Random Oracle
authors: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information-theoretic MPC among [MATH] parties with [MATH] corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit [MATH] with [MATH] online communication in the preprocessing model and [MATH] communication in the honest majority setting. Damg{\aa}rd, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same [MATH] lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an [MATH] communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when [MATH], beating the information-theoretic bound. We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with [MATH] communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits [MATH] such that every blackbox protocol with [MATH] quantum communication must perform [MATH] cryptographic operations.
tldr: The paper studies communication-complexity lower bounds for secure multi-party computation (MPC) in classical and quantum settings, including random-oracle models and quantum communication.
motivation: While information-theoretic MPC communication bounds are known to be tight for certain functionalities, it is unclear whether random oracles or quantum communication can circumvent these bounds under symmetric-key assumptions.
method: The authors prove lower bounds for MPC with preprocessing in the random oracle model, extend them to quantum-accessible random oracles and quantum communication, and construct matching or improved protocols for degree-2 polynomials and two-party computations.
result: A random oracle cannot reduce online communication for MPC with preprocessing; honest-majority MPC can beat information-theoretic bounds for degree-2 polynomials; quantum communication alone cannot improve information-theoretic protocols, but with post-quantum one-way functions a two-party protocol beats the lower bounds, at the cost of many cryptographic operations.
conclusion: Quantum communication and random oracles offer nuanced trade-offs for secure MPC, with some communication savings possible only under computational assumptions and with additional cryptographic overhead.

title: Pump Quantization Changes Optimal Measurements For Quantum Sensing
authors: S. A. Wadood, L. Bello, T. Ilias, J. W. Fleischer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard analyses of quantum phase sensing often neglect the overhead of generating squeezed-light by treating the pump as an undepleted classical resource. Realistically, the pump is a quantum object that undergoes significant depletion and entangles with the produced squeezed light, raising the question of how the crossover from a classical to a quantum pump limits the quantum advantage in sensing. Contrary to prior analyses, we show that quantum advantage persists despite pump quantization, but depends critically on the nonlinear [MATH] source dynamics. In particular, we demonstrate that Heisenberg scaling emerges in the regime of strong pump depletion, rather than maximum signal squeezing. At maximum squeezing, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for interferometric sensing of an unknown phase scales as [MATH], where [MATH] is the pump photon number, surpassing the shot-noise limit but establishing that squeezing itself is insufficient to attain Heisenberg scaling of [MATH]. At maximal pump depletion, where the signal flux is maximized, the QFI scales as [MATH]. In this regime, standard photon counting is suboptimal, while a joint nonlinear measurement of the entire pump-signal system is shown to achieve Heisenberg scaling. Our work shows that pump quantization changes both the optimal operating point and the measurement strategies required to preserve a realistic quantum advantage in phase estimation and, more broadly, many-body quantum dynamics.
tldr: The paper analyzes quantum phase sensing with a quantized pump, showing that Heisenberg scaling can arise from strong pump depletion and requires joint nonlinear pump-signal measurements rather than standard photon counting.
motivation: Standard quantum sensing analyses treat the squeezed-light pump as an undepleted classical resource, ignoring pump depletion and pump-signal entanglement; the authors ask how a realistic quantum pump affects the achievable quantum advantage.
method: They model the nonlinear source dynamics with a quantized pump and evaluate the quantum Fisher information for interferometric phase sensing, comparing optimal measurement strategies across squeezing and depletion regimes.
result: Quantum advantage persists despite pump quantization, but the scaling changes: at maximum squeezing the QFI surpasses the shot-noise limit without reaching Heisenberg scaling, while strong pump depletion yields Heisenberg scaling and requires a joint nonlinear measurement of the pump-signal system.
conclusion: Pump quantization changes both the optimal operating point and the required measurement strategy for realistic quantum-enhanced phase estimation.

title: The Impact Of Internal Electric Fields On Accurate Diamond Magnetometry
authors: Jack Faller, Daphne Freda Gavras, Andrew Lowther, Romain Ruhlmann, Lilian Childress
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center spin ensembles are a promising platform for accurate vector magnetometry, as they offer measurements referenced to a spin Hamiltonian in an anisotropic crystal with native vector sensing capabilities. However, charged dopants within the diamond produce random internal electric fields (RIEFs) that shift NV spin-transition frequencies, and their impact on the accuracy of NV magnetometry has not been investigated. Here, we characterize RIEFs' effect on NV spin-transition spectra and propose an analytical fitting function to improve accuracy in their presence. We build a Monte Carlo RIEF model that reproduces the asymmetric lineshapes observed in experimental optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, and use it as a testbed to quantify RIEF-induced errors by simulating ODMR spectra including RIEFs and comparing reconstructed magnetic fields to the known model input. With standard analysis approaches, we observe systematic errors exceeding the g-factor uncertainty in fields below [MATH] 5 mT, while the proposed fitting function reduces the error by nearly an order of magnitude. Our results demonstrate that RIEFs can play a significant role in the systematic error budget for NV magnetometry, and offer a path towards improved accuracy in NV quantum sensing.
tldr: The paper models how random internal electric fields from charged dopants distort NV-center ODMR spectra and proposes a fitting function to reduce systematic errors in diamond vector magnetometry.
motivation: NV ensembles are promising for accurate vector magnetometry, but random internal electric fields shift spin-transition frequencies, and their impact on magnetometry accuracy had not been systematically characterized.
method: The authors build a Monte Carlo model of random internal electric fields, reproduce asymmetric experimental ODMR lineshapes, and simulate ODMR spectra to compare reconstructed magnetic fields with known inputs using standard and improved fitting approaches.
result: Standard analysis shows systematic errors exceeding the g-factor uncertainty below about 5 mT, while the proposed analytical fitting function reduces the RIEF-induced error by nearly an order of magnitude.
conclusion: Random internal electric fields are a significant systematic error source for NV magnetometry, and the proposed fitting method offers a practical path to improved accuracy in NV quantum sensing.

title: Initialization-controlled Fault Sensitivity And Force-balance Plateaus In Noisy Variational Quantum Optimization
authors: Longhui Shen, Fangzhou Jin, Bin Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study deep variational circuits for a periodic Heisenberg chain under local gate depolarization, at depths where noiseless training is coherently exact. Full-width initializations reach low coherent error faster than circuits with confined transverse generators, but incur a larger noise shift and need an order of magnitude more updates for noisy convergence. In many-body-localization-inspired initialization, bounding the initial transverse generator amplitudes keeps the operator support localized and suffices for low-fragility optimization, so longitudinal disorder and Floquet layer repetition are unnecessary. The fault-erasure fraction, the mean fraction of coherent energy removed per fault, sets the effective visibility through a parameter-free exponential model. Full-width circuits start with delocalized operator support, and once coherent energy builds up, each fault erases nearly all of it. Initially, their noise-induced gradient almost uniformly attenuates the coherent gradient, so coherent descent proceeds at the noiseless rate. They then stall on a high-noise force-balance plateau, where finite coherent and noise-induced gradients cancel to first order. At late times all initializations reach the same fault-erasure fraction and noisy-error band, but operator support contracts more slowly, at a rate set by the plateau residence time.
tldr: The paper studies how initialization choices in noisy deep variational circuits for a periodic Heisenberg chain affect fault sensitivity, gradient behavior, and convergence to a force-balance plateau under local depolarizing noise.
motivation: Variational quantum optimization is limited by noise, and the authors aim to understand how initial operator support and circuit structure control fault-induced errors and noisy optimization dynamics.
method: They analyze deep variational circuits with different initializations, including full-width and many-body-localization-inspired schemes, under local gate depolarization, tracking coherent error, noise-induced gradients, fault-erasure fraction, and operator support.
result: Full-width initializations reduce coherent error quickly but suffer larger noise shifts and require many more updates; bounding initial transverse generator amplitudes can localize operator support and enable low-fragility optimization without longitudinal disorder or Floquet repetition.
conclusion: The fault-erasure fraction sets effective visibility via a parameter-free exponential model, and late-time behavior converges across initializations while operator support contraction depends on plateau residence time.

title: Quantum Banking System For Secure Cash Withdrawal
authors: Vineet Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum-secure withdrawal framework is presented by replacing reproducible classical credentials with quantum tokens for authentication. The protocol integrates token generation, authentication, and verification into the existing banking workflow using experimentally motivated quantum control techniques. This mitigates card cloning, credential theft, and counterfeiting.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantum-token-based authentication framework for secure cash withdrawal in banking systems.
motivation: Classical banking credentials are vulnerable to cloning, theft, and counterfeiting, motivating the replacement of reproducible credentials with quantum tokens.
method: The protocol integrates quantum token generation, authentication, and verification into existing banking workflows using experimentally motivated quantum control techniques.
result: The framework is claimed to mitigate card cloning, credential theft, and counterfeiting by making credentials non-reproducible.
conclusion: The work is an applied quantum-secure banking proposal, but it lacks rigorous information-theoretic security analysis and is only tangentially related to core quantum information research.

title: On The Hardness Of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership And Optimization
authors: Adam Husted Kjelstr{\o}m, Jaco van de Pol, Andreas Pavlogiannis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is an indispensable component of the quantum software stack, used to reduce noise, maximize performance, alleviate costs of quantum error correction, or target specific hardware. A related problem is approximate membership: for a fixed set of unitaries [MATH], decide whether a given circuit [MATH] is within distance [MATH] of a unitary in [MATH] under some metric [MATH]. Membership is a special case of optimization, where [MATH] is a set of unitaries implementable at no cost (e.g., with noise-minimal circuits, or without magic states). Janzing, Wocjan, and Beth (Int. J. Quantum Inf., 2005) showed that, for the operator metric, the case [MATH] (approximate identity) is QMA-complete when [MATH] is promised to be either close to the identity or far from it. We generalize this setting in three directions: (i) promise-free inputs, (ii) besides [MATH], sets [MATH] containing only Clifford unitaries, or only generalized permutation matrices (i.e., no superposition), and (iii) the trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics. We show that, in all cases, approximate membership is PP-hard for wide ranges of [MATH], provided [MATH]'s gate-set can implement Clifford+T, as the gate-sets of standard hardware do. If [MATH], or if [MATH] contains only generalized permutation matrices, [MATH], and [MATH] is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds for all non-trivial [MATH]. If [MATH] and [MATH] is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds even for circuits over classical-reversible gate-sets. Our results indicate that approximate membership is harder over promise-free inputs than the QMA-complete promise version, and that this hardness persists across quantum resources (any gates, non-Clifford, superposition) and distance metrics. They directly imply PP-hardness of circuit optimization when minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth or count.
tldr: The paper proves PP-hardness of promise-free approximate quantum circuit membership and optimization for Clifford+T gate sets, Clifford-only sets, and generalized permutation sets under trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics.
motivation: Circuit optimization is central to the quantum software stack, and prior work (Janzing–Wocjan–Beth) established QMA-completeness for approximate identity membership under a promise; the authors ask how hard the problem becomes without promises and for restricted unitary sets and alternative distance metrics.
method: Complexity-theoretic reductions extending the Janzing–Wocjan–Beth framework to promise-free inputs, restricted unitary classes (Clifford-only, generalized permutations), and multiple metrics (trace-based, spectral, operator), assuming gate sets that can implement Clifford+T.
result: Approximate membership is PP-hard in all considered settings for wide ranges of the precision parameter, including classical-reversible gate sets for trace-based distances, and these hardness results lift to circuit optimization when minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth or count.
conclusion: Approximate membership without promises is strictly harder than the QMA-complete promise version, and the hardness persists across quantum resources and distance metrics, implying PP-hardness of practical circuit optimization objectives.

title: Entanglement-Aware Quantum Circuit Optimization Through Globally Optimal Partitioning
authors: Gregory Morse, Muhammad Al Farizi, Jakab N\'adori, L\'aszl\'o Hajas, Tam\'as Kozsik, Peter Rakyta
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a scalable framework for globally optimal quantum-circuit partitioning and entanglement-aware block resynthesis. The partitioning problem is formulated as an integer linear program over qubit-feasible convex subcircuits, supporting objectives such as minimizing the number of partitions or a weighted execution cost. The resulting partition selection is exact over the enumerated feasible candidates and their computed costs when the ILP is solved to proven optimality. The selected partitions are resynthesized using an operator-Schmidt rank (OSR) based synthesis technique, which exploits their internal entanglement structure. We compare the end-to-end integer linear programming (ILP)--OSR workflow with BQSKit while identifying their different routing methods, and separately compare local OSR and BQSKit synthesis on matched three- and four-qubit unitaries. On the frozen sample of 772 local unitary targets, OSR produces 741 verified syntheses versus 617 for BQSKit, and matches or improves the CNOT count in all 617 jointly verified pairs. These results demonstrate that globally optimal partition selection combined with entanglement-aware resynthesis improves circuit quality and extends block-based optimization to problem sizes that are impractical for existing optimization workflows.
tldr: A scalable framework combines integer linear programming for globally optimal circuit partitioning with operator-Schmidt-rank-based block resynthesis to cut CNOT counts in quantum circuit compilation.
motivation: Block-based circuit optimization depends heavily on how a circuit is partitioned and how each block is resynthesized; existing heuristic partitioning and synthesis tools leave quality and scalability on the table.
method: The partitioning problem is cast as an integer linear program over qubit-feasible convex subcircuits with objectives such as minimal partition count or weighted execution cost, and selected blocks are resynthesized with an operator-Schmidt-rank synthesis exploiting their internal entanglement structure; benchmarks compare the ILP-OSR workflow against BQSKit and local OSR vs. BQSKit synthesis on matched 3- and 4-qubit unitaries.
result: On 772 local unitary targets, OSR yields 741 verified syntheses versus 617 for BQSKit and matches or improves CNOT counts in all 617 jointly verified pairs, while the ILP partitioning extends block optimization to sizes impractical for existing workflows.
conclusion: Entanglement-aware, globally optimal partitioning plus OSR resynthesis improves compiled circuit quality and scalability, offering a practical compiler-level advantage rather than new information-theoretic insight.

title: Hardware-Aware Design And Layout Selection In Quantum Reservoir Computing For Insurance Claims Forecasting
authors: Ren\'ata Rusn\'akov\'a, Eugen \v{s}lapak, Gaurav K. Pandey, Juraj Gazda
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines.
