On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.
tldr: A six-qubit quantum reservoir computer is benchmarked for motor-insurance claim forecasting and transferred to IBM Kingston with hardware-aware layout selection.
motivation: The authors ask whether small quantum reservoir computing models can competitively forecast real temporal data and whether their performance survives noisy hardware execution.
method: Five hardware-native reservoir candidates using Trotterized Ising dynamics were frozen via memory, measurement robustness, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening; they were then compared with ridge regression and classical baselines, and tested on IBM Kingston using hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit layouts.
result: Ideal simulations reached RMSEs of 5.66–6.12 claims/day versus 5.36 for ridge regression, with four candidates not significantly different; hardware-aware layouts consistently beat Qiskit layouts and reduced transfer distortion.
conclusion: Small quantum reservoir computers can be competitive on this forecasting task, and hardware-aware layout selection improves transfer consistency to noisy superconducting hardware.

title: High-fidelity Quantum Gate Learning Via Physics-informed Neural Networks
authors: Luis Fabra, Cristian E. Susa, Alcides Montoya, Ariel Norambuena
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of [MATH] for Hadamard and values between [MATH] and [MATH] for controlled-NOT under [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of [MATH] coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below [MATH]. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at [MATH] preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity [MATH] at [MATH] and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.
tldr: The paper uses physics-informed neural networks to learn smooth control fields for high-fidelity one- and two-qubit quantum gates and tests them under weak dissipation.
motivation: High-fidelity quantum gate synthesis requires control fields that satisfy model dynamics, physical constraints, and robustness to noise, motivating automated optimization methods.
method: A PINN is trained on the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with a loss combining gate error, physical constraints, regularization, and multiple initial conditions, then validated with Haar-random states, Lindblad simulations, and Chebyshev control representations.
result: The approach achieves low average gate infidelity for Hadamard and CNOT gates, reproduces first-order fidelity loss under weak dephasing and amplitude damping, and compresses learned controls into compact Chebyshev expansions and square-pulse playback.
conclusion: PINN-based control learning can synthesize compact high-fidelity quantum gates and characterize control resources, though its contribution is primarily quantum control and gate synthesis rather than a core information-theoretic or thermodynamic result.

title: Hybrid Quantum--Classical Pauli-Correlator Architecture For Image Reconstruction
authors: Siddhartha Patra Sparsho Chakraborty
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the Pauli-Correlator Autoencoder (PCAE), a hybrid quantum--classical architecture for image reconstruction. PCAE splits an image into patches and compresses each patch as a matrix product state (MPS). A small quantum circuit turns each compressed patch into a few measured numbers, and a classical neural network rebuilds the patch from these numbers and the patch position. A learnable energy term, taken from physics, is added to training and tracked as training proceeds. Two versions place the six qubits on a line (PCAE1D) or on a grid (PCAE2D). An averaging step makes the PCAE2D features follow rotations and reflections of the image exactly. Trained on one image at a time, PCAE2D rebuilds images from six public datasets with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 25.8 to 41.6 decibels. On CIFAR-10 images not used in training, a formula-based stand-in for the PCAE2D features performs within 1 decibel of several simpler classical methods. Five trained models also run on real IBM quantum computers without retraining, and rebuild images at 25.90 to 31.52 decibels. A short argument and a synthetic test show that, with a linear final layer, measuring qubits in pairs is needed for targets built from products of inputs. These results show that PCAE works as a hybrid model that rebuilds varied images and runs on today's quantum hardware at the six-qubit scale.
tldr: The paper introduces a hybrid quantum-classical Pauli-Correlator Autoencoder that compresses image patches as matrix product states, processes them with a six-qubit circuit, and reconstructs images using a classical neural network.
motivation: The authors aim to demonstrate a practical hybrid quantum-classical model for image reconstruction that can run on current small-scale quantum hardware.
method: Images are split into patches, each compressed into an MPS representation; a small quantum circuit maps each patch to a few measurement outcomes, which a classical network uses to reconstruct the patch, with a physics-inspired energy term added to training.
result: PCAE2D achieves PSNR of 25.8–41.6 dB on six public datasets and 25.90–31.52 dB when deployed on IBM quantum computers without retraining; a formula-based stand-in is within 1 dB of simpler classical methods on unseen CIFAR-10 images.
conclusion: The work shows a working six-qubit hybrid quantum-classical image-reconstruction pipeline, but its contribution is primarily applied quantum machine learning rather than a foundational result in quantum information theory.

title: Lower Bounds For Adaptive Relaxed Locally Decodable Codes Via The Capped Horvitz--Thompson Estimator
authors: Guy Goldberg, Tom Gur, Sidhant Saraogi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a nearly optimal lower bound on the blocklength of general relaxed locally decodable codes (RLDCs), extending the result of [GGS26] to nonlinear encodings and adaptive decoders with two-sided error. Namely, we show that any [MATH]-query RLDC [MATH] must satisfy [MATH], closely matching the upper bound of [MATH] by Ben-Sasson, Goldreich, Harsha, Sudan, and Vadhan (STOC 2004). Our proof reduces showing RLDC lower bounds to estimating the output distribution of adaptive decoders. To this end, we introduce a capped Horvitz--Thompson estimator with uniformly bounded discrete derivatives on the [MATH]-biased cube. We establish its concentration of measure via self-bounding inequalities and control the downward bias induced by capping through a spreadness argument.
tldr: The paper proves a nearly optimal lower bound on the blocklength of general relaxed locally decodable codes (RLDCs) for nonlinear encodings and adaptive two-sided-error decoders, matching the classical Ben-Sasson–Goldreich–Harsha–Sudan–Vadhan upper bound.
motivation: Prior RLDC lower bounds (e.g., GGS26) only covered restricted settings such as linear encodings or non-adaptive decoders, leaving open whether adaptivity and nonlinearity could beat the known blocklength bounds.
method: The authors reduce RLDC lower bounds to estimating the output distribution of adaptive decoders, introducing a capped Horvitz–Thompson estimator with uniformly bounded discrete derivatives on the biased cube, proving concentration via self-bounding inequalities and controlling capping-induced downward bias with a spreadness argument.
result: Any q-query RLDC is shown to require blocklength nearly matching the STOC 2004 upper bound, establishing near-optimality of relaxed locally decodable codes even in the fully general adaptive, nonlinear, two-sided-error setting.
conclusion: The work closes the gap between upper and lower bounds for RLDCs, and the capped Horvitz–Thompson estimator technique may be of independent interest for analyzing adaptive query algorithms.

title: A New Class Of Optimal Binary Linear Complementary Pairs Of Codes
authors: Jing Chen Yansheng Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The construction of optimal binary linear complementary pair (LCP) has recently attracted considerable attention in coding theory. Based on the Belov codes, this paper proposes a novel construction of optimal binary LCPs with [MATH], extending our previous work on [MATH]. Our results not only yield abundant new optimal binary LCPs with flexible parameters, but also enable more optimal binary LCPs with smaller minimum distances.
tldr: The paper constructs a new family of optimal binary linear complementary pairs (LCPs) of codes based on Belov codes, yielding flexible parameters and improved minimum distances.
motivation: Optimal binary LCPs have attracted attention in coding theory, and prior constructions (the authors' earlier work) were limited in parameter range and minimum distance; the authors seek broader and better constructions.
method: They generalize the Belov-code-based construction to a new class of binary LCPs with extended parameter ranges, analyzing the resulting minimum distances and optimality conditions.
result: The construction produces abundant new optimal binary LCPs with flexible parameters and also yields optimal LCPs with smaller minimum distances than previously achievable.
conclusion: The new Belov-code-based family enlarges the known space of optimal binary LCPs and improves the achievable parameter trade-offs, with relevance primarily to classical coding theory.

title: Making Every Edit Count: Efficient Binary Edit Correction At The Gilbert-Varshamov Bound
authors: Ryan Gabrys, Shubhransh Singhvi, Eitan Yaakobi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04023v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct binary codes that attain the classical Gilbert-Varshamov redundancy guarantee for a fixed number of edit errors, with deterministic polynomial-time construction, encoding, and decoding. For every fixed integer [MATH] and all sufficiently large block lengths [MATH], our codes correct any combination of at most [MATH] insertions, deletions, and substitutions in total, with redundancy at most [MATH]. All algorithms run in polynomial time in [MATH] for fixed [MATH], and decoding recovers the original information message. This realizes the classical counting guarantee algorithmically without enumerating the exponentially large space of binary words.
tldr: Constructs binary codes with deterministic polynomial-time construction, encoding and decoding that achieve the Gilbert-Varshamov redundancy for a fixed number of insertions, deletions and substitutions.
motivation: The Gilbert-Varshamov bound guarantees the existence of good edit-correcting codes, but realizing this counting guarantee with explicit, efficiently decodable constructions has remained open.
method: Explicit combinatorial code construction combined with deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms that avoid enumerating the exponential space of binary words.
result: For every fixed number of edits and all sufficiently large block lengths, the codes correct any combination of at most that many insertions, deletions and substitutions with redundancy at most the GV bound, with all algorithms polynomial time.
conclusion: The classical counting bound for edit correction is made algorithmic, yielding explicit near-optimal binary edit-correcting codes.

title: Pairwise Distortion Distribution With Graph-Based Importance Sampling For Quantization Error And Intrinsic Dimension Estimation
authors: Xi Chen, Carl Nuzman, Shirin Jalali
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying the dimensionality of data is a fundamental need in machine learning and signal processing applications such as representation learning, data compression, and inverse problems, where the extrinsic dimension in which the data is presented can be very different from the intrinsic dimension that determines the operational performance. Various concepts, such as R\'enyi information dimension, rate-distortion dimension, and quantization dimension are useful here. Despite their theoretical significance, estimating these measures are challenging given their asymptotic definitions. Recent research has shown that analyzing the pairwise distortion distribution (PDD) of a data source can provide a tractable lower bound on the distortion of random codebook quantization, from which a tractable notion of intrinsic dimension can be derived. In this paper we extend this line of research in three main ways. First, we develop a related upper bound on distortion of random codebook quantization. Second, we improve the computability of both the lower and upper bounds, using a graph-based adaptive importance sampling approach. Third, we leverage the bounds to define new notions of intrinsic dimension which form upper and lower bounds on the R\'enyi information dimension, rate-distortion dimension, and quantization dimension, and which can be empirically estimated from unknown data sources. We illustrate the concepts by analyzing several artificial and empirical distributions.
tldr: The paper develops graph-based adaptive importance sampling to compute upper and lower bounds on random-codebook quantization distortion via pairwise distortion distributions, yielding new empirically estimable notions of intrinsic dimension.
motivation: Intrinsic dimension measures such as Rényi information dimension, rate-distortion dimension, and quantization dimension are theoretically important but hard to estimate because they are defined asymptotically, so tractable finite-sample bounds are needed.
method: Extends the pairwise distortion distribution (PDD) framework by deriving a matching upper bound on random codebook quantization distortion and using graph-based adaptive importance sampling to make both bounds computable from data.
result: The bounds are shown to bracket the Rényi information dimension, rate-distortion dimension, and quantization dimension, giving new intrinsic-dimension estimators that are validated on artificial and real empirical distributions.
conclusion: PDD-based bounds with importance sampling provide a practical, computable route to estimating dimensionality of unknown data sources, though the work is purely classical information theory and signal processing.

title: Estimating The Generator Of Matrix Exponential Time-series
authors: Jon\'a\v{s} Fuksa, Jens Eisert, Ingo Roth
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The achievable precision in estimating the spectrum of a time-series signal that is promised to be sparse in Fourier space deteriorates rapidly as the spectral peaks get closer together, as soon as we introduce noise. Here, we study the related task of generator estimation: estimating the generator of a matrix exponential time-series and its eigenvalues. We obtain rigorous non-asymptotic precision guarantees on genESPRIT, a practical algorithm solving generator estimation, and show that this task can be solved with precision independent of the spectral spacing. The guarantees are complemented by a Cram\'er--Rao analysis of a relaxation of the problem. In particular, in the case of unitary data with bounded additive noise with effective entrywise variance [MATH], we show that genESPRIT estimates the associated propagator matrix in Frobenius norm with precision scaling as [MATH] in the length of the time-series [MATH] and matrix dimension [MATH], matching the corresponding spectrum-independent Cram\'er--Rao standard deviation scaling up to logarithmic factors. We prove that the matching distance error in the spectrum estimated by genESPRIT scales as [MATH], which we compare to the lower bound on the corresponding Cram\'er--Rao bound with the asymptotic standard deviation scaling [MATH]. These guarantees provide the first rigorous bounds on solving the generator estimation problem. As the matrix exponential time-series can be obtained from linearly independent vector time-series by concatenation, this work opens up a new direction in spectral estimation, which circumvents the problem of crowded spectra, under the additional assumption of linear independence.
tldr: The paper introduces and rigorously analyzes genESPRIT for estimating the generator and eigenvalues of a matrix exponential time-series.
motivation: Standard sparse spectral estimation degrades when spectral peaks are close and noise is present; the authors seek spacing-independent precision for generator estimation.
method: They derive non-asymptotic guarantees for genESPRIT and complement them with a Cramér-Rao analysis of a relaxed problem, including unitary data with bounded additive noise.
result: genESPRIT estimates the propagator matrix in Frobenius norm with precision scaling favorably in time-series length and dimension, and its spectral matching-distance error matches Cramér-Rao scaling up to logarithmic factors.
conclusion: This provides the first rigorous bounds for generator estimation and opens a spectral-estimation direction that avoids crowded-spectra limitations under linear independence assumptions.

title: Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz For The Toda Chain From Inverse Scattering Transform
authors: Alberto Brollo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) procedure developed by Yang-Yang provides the free energy functional to be minimized via a variational problem. Their result not only gives the correct thermodynamics, but it also sets the framework for Generalized Hydrodynamics. Originally developed for quantum systems, this procedure has been recently successfully applied to (integrable) classical particle systems. However, this has never been done for classical field theories: no classical derivation has consistently accounted for solitons, breathers, radiation (dispersive modes), and their mutual interactions. We here derive the TBA equations for the Toda chain directly from its inverse scattering transform. This results in solitonic modes interacting with radiation, extending the soliton gas picture. We provide numerical verification of our equations against well established TBA equations in terms of particle modes. We expect the same procedure should apply to KdV, and pure radiative models as defocusing NLS and Sinh-Gordon, while we discuss current limitations in other models such as focusing NLS (and Ablowitz-Ladik) and Sine-Gordon.
tldr: The paper derives Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz equations for the classical Toda chain directly from its inverse scattering transform, incorporating solitons, breathers, radiation, and their interactions.
motivation: Yang-Yang TBA has been applied to integrable classical particle systems but not consistently to classical field theories with solitonic and radiative modes; this work aims to fill that gap.
method: The author uses the inverse scattering transform of the Toda chain to formulate TBA equations describing interacting solitonic modes and radiation, then verifies the equations numerically against known particle-mode TBA results.
result: The derived TBA equations extend the soliton gas picture by including soliton-radiation interactions, and numerical checks confirm agreement with established TBA formulations for particle modes.
conclusion: The procedure is expected to generalize to KdV and purely radiative models such as defocusing NLS and Sinh-Gordon, while limitations remain for focusing NLS, Ablowitz-Ladik, and Sine-Gordon.

title: Adaptive Qubit Encoding For Continuous-Variable Quantum Optimization
authors: Samuele Cavinato, Marco Tesoro, Gianluca Morettini, Marta Paiusco, Alessandro Scaggion, Simone Montangero, Ilaria Siloi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing continuous-variable functions on qubit-based quantum hardware requires a finite representation of the search space and a solver-compatible representation of the objective function. Fixed-grid discretizations provide a direct encoding, but restrict the search to a predefined range and resolution; at the same time, constructing a compact Hamiltonian for a general continuous-variable objective can be impractical. Here, we introduce a framework for continuous-variable optimization tailored to qubit-based quantum architectures. The method combines an adaptive discretization with an iterative local mapping of the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian. We assess the approach on unconstrained and constrained instances of the [MATH]-dimensional Gramacy-Lee benchmark, and on a proof-of-concept inverse-planning problem in intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for cancer treatment. The results show that this framework can produce competitive solutions, supporting its use as a flexible mapping strategy for continuous-variable optimization in qubit-based quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines.
tldr: The paper introduces an adaptive discretization and iterative local spin-glass Hamiltonian mapping framework for continuous-variable optimization on qubit-based quantum hardware.
motivation: Fixed-grid encodings restrict search range and resolution, while constructing compact Hamiltonians for general continuous objectives is impractical, motivating flexible encodings for qubit-based optimization.
method: The approach combines adaptive discretization with iterative local mapping of the objective function onto an effective spin-glass Hamiltonian, tested on Gramacy-Lee benchmark instances and an IMRT inverse-planning problem.
result: The framework produces competitive solutions on unconstrained and constrained benchmark instances and in the radiotherapy proof-of-concept, supporting its use as a flexible mapping strategy.
conclusion: Adaptive qubit encoding may enable practical continuous-variable optimization in quantum and quantum-inspired pipelines, though the work is application-oriented and outside the listed core research directions.

title: Reasoning About Shared-Qubit Concurrency In Quantum Computing
authors: Mingsheng Ying
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop a semantic model for the parallel execution of quantum circuits, providing a formal foundation for studying shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing. As in classical shared-memory concurrency, parallel quantum circuits may interfere with one another through operations on shared qubits. However, quantum entanglement and the noncommutativity of quantum operations introduce additional challenges for reasoning about their correctness. To address these challenges, we generalise the classical Owicki-Gries method to quantum computing at the level of quantum circuits. Our approach enables compositional reasoning about parallel quantum circuits by separating the verification of individual components from the analysis of interference between them. We formulate proof rules for establishing the correctness of parallel quantum circuits and prove their soundness with respect to the proposed semantic model.
tldr: The paper develops a semantic model and proof rules for compositional reasoning about parallel quantum circuits that share qubits.
motivation: Parallel quantum circuits can interfere via shared qubits, and entanglement plus noncommuting operations make correctness reasoning harder than in classical shared-memory concurrency.
method: It generalizes the classical Owicki-Gries method to quantum circuits, separating verification of individual components from analysis of interference, and proves soundness relative to a semantic model.
result: The paper formulates proof rules for establishing correctness of parallel quantum circuits and proves their soundness.
conclusion: This provides a formal foundation for shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing, but it is a programming-language/verification contribution rather than a quantum information or thermodynamics result.

title: Reducing The Arithmetic Cost Of Quantum Derivative Pricing With Language-model Circuit Design
authors: Hoong Chun Lau Monit Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation can estimate expected discounted payoffs with quadratically fewer oracle calls than Monte Carlo, but each call requires coherent computation. We use language-model-assisted circuit design to reduce reversible payoff arithmetic for a three-asset worst-of autocallable and a target accrual redemption forward (TARF). The constructions retain compact integer representations of market paths alongside contract history, reconstructing quantities temporarily for contract decisions and payoff-angle evaluation. Relative to matched internal references, the factor-sum autocallable and windowed TARF circuits reduce the product of Toffoli count and peak logical qubits [MATH] by factors of 2.39 and 4.84, respectively. At a second autocallable setting, fresh search recovers a 1.35-fold saving after the tested fixed adaptation loses its advantage. For the factor-sum circuit, we prove exact coherent execution of its integer specification for every input, incoming accumulator and measurement record, with clean workspace and phase cancellation. A separate lattice calculation gives a numerical angle-tolerance-violation probability of 6.248e-8 and evaluates pricing bias under the declared loading law, with bounded omission but no certified numerical enclosure. The results connect compact representations to lower-cost payoff arithmetic and separately assessed logical and financial correctness. Their resource scope excludes loading, payoff rotation and estimation.
tldr: The paper uses language-model-assisted circuit design to reduce reversible arithmetic costs in quantum amplitude estimation for derivative pricing contracts.
motivation: Quantum amplitude estimation can price financial derivatives with fewer oracle calls than Monte Carlo, but coherent payoff arithmetic is expensive and needs optimization.
method: The authors design compact integer representations of market paths and contract history, reconstructing quantities only when needed for contract decisions and payoff-angle evaluation, with language-model assistance for circuit design.
result: Relative to matched internal references, the circuits reduce the product of Toffoli count and peak logical qubits by factors of 2.39 and 4.84 for an autocallable and a TARF, respectively, and they prove exact coherent execution for the factor-sum circuit.
conclusion: The work connects compact representations to lower-cost quantum payoff arithmetic and separately assesses logical and financial correctness, but its scope excludes loading, payoff rotation, and estimation.

title: Broken-Symmetry Reference States For Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization With Near-DMRG Accuracy
authors: Kunal Kumar, Tomonori Shirakawa, Boseong Kim, Ryo Wakizaka, Ikko Hamamura, Mitsuhisa Sato, Seiji Yunoki, Mario Motta, Hiroshi Horii, Yuri Kobayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) accuracy remains limited for strongly correlated systems like iron-sulfur clusters. This accuracy heavily depends on the mean-field reference state, which determines the sampling ansatz and configuration-recovery target. We extend the qcsc-prefect workflow to support a broken-symmetry unrestricted Hartree-Fock (BS-UHF) starting point, derived from atom-localized antiferromagnetic initial guesses. For the [MATH] cubane (54 electrons, 36 orbitals, 72 data qubits; 88 total qubits), this lowers the mean-field reference by [MATH] mHa relative to the Restricted Hartree-Fock (RHF) solution (-327.0809 vs. -326.5474 Ha). Combined with deep multi-step configuration recovery on ROQUO GPU nodes at subspace dimension [MATH], we reach [MATH] Ha. This is 4.3 mHa above the finite-[MATH] DMRG value (-327.2393952 Ha) and [MATH] mHa below a previous same-active-space RHF-reference SQD calculation. Extrapolating to the [MATH] limit via a Gaussian-in-log [MATH] fitting ansatz gives an asymptotic estimate [MATH] Ha [MATH] mHa, just 0.33 mHa above our discarded-weight-extrapolated DMRG estimate ([MATH] Ha [MATH] mHa), well within their combined [MATH] uncertainty. We characterize the determinant-subspace composition driving convergence, show matching validation on [MATH], and report multi-HPC execution on Fugaku, Miyabi-G, and ROQUO. We conclude that reference-state preparation, rather than subspace size alone, is a key driver of SQD energy accuracy under strong electronic correlation.
tldr: The paper improves sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) for strongly correlated Fe-S cubane systems by using broken-symmetry UHF reference states derived from atom-localized antiferromagnetic guesses, achieving near-DMRG accuracy.
motivation: SQD accuracy on strongly correlated transition-metal clusters is limited by the mean-field reference state, which fixes the sampling ansatz and configuration-recovery target; better references are needed to close the gap to DMRG.
method: The qcsc-prefect workflow is extended to accept BS-UHF starting points from atom-localized antiferromagnetic initial guesses, combined with deep multi-step configuration recovery at large subspace dimension on GPU nodes, plus Gaussian-in-log extrapolation to the infinite-subspace limit.
result: The BS-UHF reference lowers the mean-field energy by roughly 0.53 Ha versus RHF, and the extrapolated SQD estimate lies only ~0.33 mHa above the extrapolated DMRG value, 4.3 mHa from the finite-subspace DMRG result.
conclusion: Reference-state preparation, rather than subspace size alone, is a key driver of SQD energy accuracy under strong electronic correlation, with validation on a second system and multi-HPC execution.

title: Approximate Synthetic Spectra Of Quantum Systems Associated With Compact Lie Groups
authors: Junyang Liu, Hang Wang, Houjin Wang, Haoran Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How can noncommuting quantum observables retain the geometry of a classical phase space? Motivated by Mumford's question on approximately macroscopically unique (AMU) states and the work of Lin and Wang, we study synthetic spectra of position--momentum and angular-momentum systems. Under the hypotheses of their AMU theorems, nonempty synthetic spectra yield AMU states. For sufficiently small [MATH], the position--momentum spectrum fills the plane, while the angular-momentum spectrum contains any prescribed ball. The latter calculation leads to compact Lie groups: we prove that highest-weight coadjoint orbits lie in regional synthetic spectra under an explicit variance bound. Function-space representations of [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] provide further examples.
tldr: The paper studies synthetic spectra of quantum position-momentum and angular-momentum systems, linking approximate macroscopic uniqueness to coadjoint orbits of compact Lie groups.
motivation: It is motivated by Mumford's question on approximately macroscopically unique states and aims to understand how noncommuting quantum observables can retain classical phase-space geometry.
method: The authors analyze synthetic spectra under AMU theorem hypotheses, compute position-momentum and angular-momentum spectra, and prove variance bounds placing highest-weight coadjoint orbits in regional synthetic spectra.
result: For small enough parameters the position-momentum spectrum fills the plane, the angular-momentum spectrum contains prescribed balls, and highest-weight coadjoint orbits lie in regional synthetic spectra under explicit variance bounds.
conclusion: The work provides mathematical results on synthetic spectra and AMU states for quantum systems tied to compact Lie groups, but it is not directly connected to the listed quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems research priorities.

title: Restricted Triangular Ice Beyond The Solvable Manifolds: Chiral Ice And The Critical Region Of Dominant Chiral Vertices
authors: Josep Batle
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study two restrictions of Baxter's symmetric twenty-vertex model on the triangular lattice, in which the three classes of vertices allowed by the ice rule carry the weights [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH]: chiral ice, in which only the twelve chiral vertices are allowed, and the model that excludes only the two alternating vertices. We show that neither model belongs to any of the known exactly solvable families of the twenty-vertex model, and we characterise chiral ice as the ice model in which every vertex has exactly one through line, a property that imposes a parity constraint along every closed lattice line. We compute the residual entropies of both models with transfer matrices on cylinders of up to twelve vertices in circumference, extrapolated with the finite-size correction predicted by conformal invariance, which we adapt to the triangular geometry and verify at two exactly solved points. The number of upward arrows crossing the cylinder is conserved, and the cost of changing it shows that both models are critical, with the long-distance behaviour of a free massless field. Chiral ice is the extreme point of a region of the phase diagram in which ordering had been suggested; along two paths through that region we find the same critical behaviour at every point, with no feature at the proposed boundary of the region. Along Baxter's exactly solved curve we obtain the corresponding exponents in closed form.
tldr: The paper studies two restricted versions of Baxter's twenty-vertex model on the triangular lattice, characterizing chiral ice and mapping its critical behavior using transfer matrices and conformal finite-size scaling.
motivation: The work investigates whether these restricted triangular ice models belong to known solvable families and examines a proposed ordered region in the phase diagram.
method: The authors use transfer-matrix calculations on cylinders up to twelve vertices in circumference, extrapolate residual entropies with conformal-invariance corrections adapted to triangular geometry, and analyze the conservation of upward-arrow crossings.
result: Neither model is exactly solvable within known families; both are critical with free massless-field long-distance behavior, and no phase-boundary feature is found along paths through the previously suggested ordered region.
conclusion: Chiral ice is an extreme critical point of the region, and the study provides closed-form exponents along Baxter's exactly solved curve, clarifying the phase behavior of these restricted vertex models.

title: On The Geometric Structure Of Hyperbolic Clifford Bundles And Associated Spin Groups
authors: Eduardo Notte-Cuello
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present the spinor structure associated with the Hyperbolic Clifford algebra of a real [MATH]-dimensional vector space [MATH], which is denoted by [MATH]. Unlike the standard Clifford algebra, the Hyperbolic Clifford algebra [MATH] simultaneously accommodates both multiforms and multivectors in a single algebraic structure, making it the natural framework---known as the ``mother algebra''---for the study of superfields in theoretical physics and for generalizing the Clifford bundle formalism to hyperbolic structures arising in gravitational theories. The orthogonal groups and orthogonal transformations associated to the hyperbolic space [MATH] are presented. The Clifford--Lipschitz group and the Pin and Spin groups associated with [MATH] are defined. Then, the frame bundle and spinor structure associated to Hyperbolic Clifford algebra is derived.
tldr: The paper constructs the spinor structure, Clifford–Lipschitz, Pin and Spin groups, frame bundle and spin structure associated with the Hyperbolic Clifford algebra of a real m-dimensional vector space, aimed at gravitational and superfield applications.
motivation: The author argues that the hyperbolic Clifford algebra ('mother algebra'), which contains both multiforms and multivectors, is the natural framework for superfields in theoretical physics and for generalizing Clifford bundle formalism to hyperbolic structures appearing in gravitational theories.
method: Purely mathematical construction: orthogonal groups and transformations of hyperbolic space are characterized, then the Clifford–Lipschitz group, Pin and Spin groups are defined, and the frame bundle and spinor structure for the hyperbolic Clifford algebra are derived.
result: A complete algebraic and bundle-theoretic presentation of the spin group and spinor structure for the hyperbolic Clifford algebra, generalizing the standard Clifford bundle formalism.
conclusion: The construction provides a geometric/differential-geometric foundation for hyperbolic Clifford bundles, with potential use in gravitational theory and superfield formalisms, but contains no quantum-information or thermodynamic content.

title: A Hybrid Quantum-classical Lattice Kinetic Scheme With Tensor-train Feedback For Incompressible Flows
authors: Yongwei Guo, Yuan Yu, Yue Yu, Yuting Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear lattice kinetic simulation requires each updated distribution to supply the velocity and gradients that determine the next step. In a quantum-classical solver, reading out the full distribution incurs work proportional to the lattice size. We construct a tensor-train (TT) interface that retains reusable classical cores at the physical amplitude scale for a full-relaxation lattice kinetic scheme. The cores supply nonlinear coefficients and prepare each quantum input. Energy-scaled propagation and coordinate recovery encode the updated distribution, and alternating least-squares reconstruction converts signed Hadamard-test overlaps into output cores by restoring a known normalization factor. The next step starts from accepted cores without replaying previous quantum evolution. Under positive, unit-sum reference coefficients, positive lower and finite upper density bounds, and Lipschitz equilibrium sensitivity, perturbation bounds relate local defects to feedback errors. Resource bounds account for classical operations, circuit execution, sampling, and verification. Classical diagnostics expose why distribution accuracy alone is insufficient: in 80-step feedback on a [MATH] grid, rank cap 4 nearly eliminates the vortex despite a final distribution error below [MATH], whereas rank cap 12 gives relative velocity error [MATH]. Four-step binomial readout simulations show that tightening core sampling tolerance threefold raises the prescribed sufficient budget from [MATH] to [MATH] shots as the result approaches the fixed-rank, fixed-sweep exact-overlap trajectory. The interface therefore provides a way to connect quantum propagation to nonlinear feedback and to assess the separate demands of compression, velocity accuracy, and readout precision.
tldr: The paper proposes a tensor-train classical interface that feeds back compressed distribution cores between quantum and classical steps of a lattice kinetic solver for incompressible fluid flows.
motivation: In quantum-classical lattice kinetic simulation, reading out the full distribution each step costs work proportional to lattice size, so a reusable compressed interface is needed to connect quantum propagation with nonlinear classical feedback.
method: The authors build a tensor-train interface retaining classical cores at physical amplitude scale, using alternating least-squares reconstruction of signed Hadamard-test overlaps to produce output cores, plus perturbation and resource bounds under stated coefficient and density assumptions.
result: Diagnostics on an 80-step feedback run show rank cap 4 nearly eliminates the vortex despite a small final distribution error, while rank cap 12 yields small relative velocity error; binomial readout simulations show a threefold tighter tolerance raises the shot budget from roughly 10^? to higher values.
conclusion: The interface links quantum propagation to nonlinear feedback and separates the demands of compression, velocity accuracy, and readout precision, but it is a numerical fluid-dynamics application rather than a quantum information or thermodynamics contribution.

title: Factorized Approximate Inverse Preconditioners In The Tensor Train Format
authors: Pau Torrente Badia, Daniel P\'erez Garc\'ia, Artur Garcia-Saez, Stefano Carignano
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a preconditioning pipeline that accelerates Tensor Train (TT) linear solvers for symmetric positive-definite problems. Extending the Factorized Sparse Approximate Inverse framework to tensor networks, we construct a preconditioner as the product of a TT operator and its transpose. This formulation is positive semidefinite for any bond dimension and truncation, and definite whenever the factor is non-singular, satisfying the mathematical requirements of the Conjugate Gradient method. We detail the construction of this preconditioner and its integration into Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG)-like linear solvers. Performance evaluations show consistent iteration reductions for anisotropic diffusion and Poisson problems across various configurations, leading to net speedups of up to 25% in ill-conditioned settings of time stepping schemes that can reuse the approximate inverses. These benchmarks were performed with the open-source Julia library DifferenTT.jl, which we also introduce in this work to provide out-of-the-box access to these preconditioned pipelines.
tldr: The authors extend the Factorized Sparse Approximate Inverse idea to the tensor-train format, building a preconditioner as the product of a TT operator and its transpose to accelerate TT linear solvers for SPD problems.
motivation: Tensor-train (DMRG-like) linear solvers converge slowly for ill-conditioned symmetric positive-definite problems, and a well-designed preconditioner that preserves the TT structure and positive (semi)definiteness would substantially reduce iteration counts.
method: They construct the preconditioner as M = A A^T in TT format, which is positive semidefinite for any bond dimension and truncation and definite when the factor is invertible, then embed it in Conjugate-Gradient-based DMRG-like solvers within a new open-source Julia library, DifferenTT.jl.
result: Benchmarks on anisotropic diffusion and Poisson problems show consistent iteration reductions, giving net speedups of up to 25% in ill-conditioned time-stepping settings where approximate inverses can be reused.
conclusion: Factorized TT approximate inverses are a practical, mathematically sound preconditioning strategy for TT linear algebra, though the contribution is a numerical-methods engineering advance rather than a result in quantum information or quantum thermodynamics.

title: Hardness Self-Amplification In Linear Algebra And Fine-Grained Cryptography
authors: Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolas Melissaris, Thejas Radhika Sajith
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the possibility of basing fine-grained cryptography on the hardness of fundamental problems in linear algebra. Our main technical contribution is a hardness self-amplification method based on random low-rank updates: we show how to turn an algorithm that solves an inverse-polynomial fraction of random linear systems into a solver which succeeds for every right-hand side of almost every matrix. Our reduction increases the runtime only linearly in the inverse of the original success probability. In particular, this yields fine-grained one-way functions from the almost worst-case hardness of linear systems over large enough fields. Using the same approach, we also obtain tighter worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix multiplication and online matrix-vector multiplication, as well as variants of our reductions that recover exact solutions from approximate algorithms, whose expected coordinate agreement is only [MATH], with inverse-quadratic dependence on [MATH] up to logarithmic factors, over every finite field. Finally, we also use it to connect the existence of fine-grained key agreement to the problem of computing the rank of a matrix: over a suitable sequence of growing characteristic-two fields, the almost-everywhere average-case hardness of rank computation (for any of a large class of distributions) implies infinitely-often fine-grained key agreement.
tldr: The paper introduces a hardness self-amplification technique based on random low-rank updates, turning weak average-case solvers for linear-algebraic problems into fine-grained one-way functions and key agreement.
motivation: Fine-grained cryptography currently relies on a narrow set of assumptions; the authors ask whether fundamental linear algebra problems (solving linear systems, matrix multiplication, rank computation) can support it.
method: A random low-rank update reduction amplifies an algorithm solving an inverse-polynomial fraction of random linear systems into one handling almost every right-hand side, with runtime growing only linearly in the inverse success probability; the same technique yields tighter worst-case to average-case reductions and approximate-to-exact solution recovery.
result: Fine-grained one-way functions follow from almost worst-case hardness of linear systems over large fields; also obtained are improved worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix multiplication and online matrix-vector multiplication, and a connection between fine-grained key agreement and average-case hardness of matrix rank over characteristic-two fields.
conclusion: Linear-algebraic hardness can serve as a basis for fine-grained cryptographic primitives, broadening the foundation of fine-grained cryptography.

title: Ray Propagation Of Circularly Polarized Light In An Inhomogeneous Medium: The Optical Magnus Effect From Maxwell's Equations
authors: Y. B. Band Igor Kuzmenko
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive the ray propagation of circularly polarized light in an inhomogeneous, isotropic and lossless medium, including the first correction to geometrical optics, the optical Magnus (spin Hall) effect. Starting from Maxwell's equations and the eikonal expansion to first order in [MATH], we show that the polarization is parallel transported along the ray, identify the Berry connection and curvature of the helicity states, and obtain a ray action in which the Berry phase appears as a correction to the optical path length. This action leads to a Hamiltonian in which the refractive index is evaluated at a position shifted by the Berry connection, [MATH]. In terms of the physical position, the equations of motion contain the Berry curvature as an anomalous velocity. We give the equivalent non-canonical bracket form, the gauge transformation, and the equivalent time-parametrized formulation with the Hamiltonian [MATH], and we state the approximations involved. The resulting ray equations are compared with analytic and numerical results. A planar interface, the helical ray in a cylindrical medium and the exact conservation of angular momentum provide checks. The formulation is set up for numerical propagation of rays in a medium with a spatially varying refractive index.
tldr: The paper derives ray propagation for circularly polarized light in an inhomogeneous isotropic medium, including the optical Magnus/spin Hall effect from Maxwell's equations via eikonal expansion.
motivation: The authors aim to give a first-principles ray-optics formulation that captures polarization-dependent corrections beyond geometrical optics, including Berry-phase and Berry-curvature effects for helicity states.
method: Starting from Maxwell's equations and a first-order eikonal expansion, they derive ray equations with a Berry connection and curvature, obtain a corrected ray action, and compare with analytic and numerical checks including a planar interface and a helical ray.
result: The formulation yields parallel transport of polarization along the ray, a shifted refractive-index Hamiltonian, an anomalous velocity from Berry curvature, and equivalent canonical, non-canonical bracket, gauge, and time-parametrized descriptions.
conclusion: The resulting ray equations provide a practical framework for numerical propagation in spatially varying refractive-index media and clarify the geometric origin of the optical Magnus effect.

title: Reconfigurable Multi-tone mmWave/THz Generation Powered By High-efficiency Kerr Parametric Oscillation
authors: Dong IL Lee, Fanqi Shen, Wenzheng Liu, Xinghe Jiang, Anika Tabassum, Alwaleed Aldhafeeri, Manas Choure, Jasmine Lu, Mona Jarrahi, Chee Wei Wong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Broadband and simultaneously accessible multi-tone millimeter-wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) signals are attractive for multi-band wireless communication and spectroscopy applications, yet their generation remains constrained by electronic bandwidth limitations and inefficient optical frequency conversion. Here, we demonstrate reconfigurable photonic generation of multi-tone mmWave/THz signals with comb spacings of 100, 200, 300, and 400 GHz, using a strongly asymmetric dual-ring silicon-nitride (SiN) microresonator and a broadband spiral plasmonic photomixer. A localized avoided-mode crossing (AMX) introduced by an auxiliary ring supports a fixed optical parametric oscillation (OPO) mode pair over an extended pump-detuning range, consistent with passive compensation of detuning-dependent phase mismatch. This enables a maximum pump-to-generated-line conversion efficiency of 67.3 % with 25.06 dB of pump depletion across different pump wavelength selections. Direct photomixing of these optical states produces simultaneous multi-frequency tones spanning 100 to 900 GHz without intermediate optical amplification. The generated carriers are further characterized through down-converted spectra, frequency-noise power spectral density (PSD), and Allan deviation measurements, yielding a -separation linewidth of 26 kHz at an observation time of 0.1 s. Optical modulation offers high radiated power levels exceeding 2 mW at 100 GHz at a duty cycle of 1 %, while mitigating thermal breakdown in the photomixer. High optical conversion efficiency, reconfigurable and selectable comb spacings, and broadband multi-tone generation on a chip-scale platform provide a compact route toward reconfigurable multi-band mmWave/THz sources for wireless communication, spectroscopy, and sensing.
tldr: The paper demonstrates chip-scale reconfigurable multi-tone mmWave/THz generation using Kerr parametric oscillation in a dual-ring SiN microresonator and plasmonic photomixing.
motivation: Broadband multi-tone mmWave/THz sources are desirable for multi-band wireless communication and spectroscopy but are limited by electronic bandwidth and inefficient optical conversion.
method: A strongly asymmetric dual-ring silicon-nitride microresonator with a localized avoided-mode crossing supports stable optical parametric oscillation, and the generated optical states are directly photomixed using a broadband spiral plasmonic photomixer.
result: The device achieves up to 67.3% pump-to-generated-line conversion efficiency, reconfigurable comb spacings of 100–400 GHz, multi-tone output spanning 100–900 GHz, and linewidth of 26 kHz with radiated power exceeding 2 mW at 100 GHz.
conclusion: This provides a compact photonic route to reconfigurable multi-band mmWave/THz sources for communication, spectroscopy, and sensing, but it is not directly related to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Capillary Coarsening Drives Re-entrant Statistical Transitions In Early Coffee-Ring Growth
authors: Dileep Mampallil Arundas Chandradasan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how nonequilibrium systems evolve between distinct statistical regimes remains a fundamental challenge in statistical physics. Here we show that particle deposition at an evaporating contact line provides an experimental realization of cooperative one-dimensional deposition, in which post-deposition capillary attraction drives particles to migrate, cluster, and coarsen. As deposition proceeds, the cluster-width distribution undergoes a striking re-entrant transition, evolving from an initial exponential form to a peaked Gamma distribution and subsequently returning to an exponential form. This dynamic transition is accompanied by a non-monotonic crossover in fluctuation scaling, [MATH], with [MATH] changing successively from [MATH] to [MATH] and back to [MATH]. Monte Carlo simulations reproduce these statistical transitions. Our results establish evaporative contact-line deposition as a simple model of correlated one-dimensional assembly and reveal how local interactions can produce re-entrant statistical behaviour in a nonequilibrium system.
tldr: The paper reports an experimental and simulational study of particle deposition at an evaporating contact line, where capillary attraction produces re-entrant statistical transitions in cluster-width distributions and fluctuation scaling.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how nonequilibrium systems evolve between distinct statistical regimes, using coffee-ring deposition as a controllable experimental realization of cooperative one-dimensional assembly.
method: They analyze particle deposition at an evaporating contact line, track cluster-width distributions and fluctuation scaling, and reproduce the observed statistical transitions with Monte Carlo simulations.
result: The cluster-width distribution transitions from exponential to peaked Gamma and back to exponential, accompanied by a non-monotonic crossover in fluctuation scaling exponents.
conclusion: Evaporative contact-line deposition provides a simple model of correlated one-dimensional assembly and shows how local capillary interactions can generate re-entrant statistical behavior in a nonequilibrium system.

title: Spectral Dynamics And Fuglede--Kadison Determinants For Wreath Products
authors: Penghui Wang, Xumin Wang, Rongwei Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate connections between operator spectra, complex dynamics, and determinants for wreath product groups. For a nontrivial finite abelian group [MATH], the natural action of [MATH] on a rooted tree produces a family of operators with a recursive structure. Applying Schur complements to this family yields a rational map on complex projective space. We determine the projective spectrum--the parameter values for which the operator pencil fails to be invertible--as the union of the Julia set of this map and an explicitly described subset of its Fatou set. We also prove that the associated Koopman representation and the left regular representation are weakly equivalent and therefore give the same projective spectrum. We then compute Fuglede--Kadison determinants for a family of operators on more general wreath products. These formulas yield injective operators with zero determinant for wreath products [MATH], where [MATH] is a discrete group admitting a nontrivial projection [MATH]. This answers negatively a question of Li and Thom about whether injectivity implies positive determinant for operators defined by matrices over complex group rings of amenable groups. For [MATH], where [MATH] is any countable torsion-free abelian group and [MATH], we prove that injectivity does imply positive determinant in every matrix size.
tldr: A pure operator-algebra paper studying projective spectra, rational maps from Schur complements, and Fuglede–Kadison determinants for wreath product groups.
motivation: Wreath product groups provide a natural setting where recursive operator families and group-ring determinants can be analyzed, and a conjecture of Li and Thom relating injectivity to positivity of Fuglede–Kadison determinants was open.
method: Schur complements along a rooted-tree action yield a rational map on complex projective space; its Julia and Fatou sets are analyzed to determine the projective spectrum, and Koopman versus left-regular representations are compared; determinants are then computed for more general wreath products.
result: The projective spectrum is characterized as the Julia set plus an explicit Fatou subset, the two representations are shown to be weakly equivalent, and injective operators with zero determinant are constructed, disproving the Li–Thom conjecture for amenable groups, while positivity is recovered for certain torsion-free abelian settings.
conclusion: The work settles a question in operator theory and group-ring determinant theory but has no evident bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Galois-modular Obstructions To The Categorification Of Near-group Fusion Rings
authors: V\'ictor Blasco
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article we establish new obstructions to the categorification of near-group fusion rings by combining the values of irreducible characters of the Grothendieck ring with the Galois symmetry of the induced unit object [MATH] in the Drinfeld center. As a result, we show that a near-group ring of type [MATH], where [MATH] is an abelian group and both [MATH] and [MATH] are odd, can only categorify if [MATH].
tldr: The paper establishes Galois-modular obstructions to categorifying certain near-group fusion rings.
motivation: Near-group fusion rings are algebraic structures relevant to fusion categories, and determining which rings admit categorification is a difficult structural problem.
method: The author combines irreducible character values of the Grothendieck ring with Galois symmetry of the induced unit object in the Drinfeld center to derive new obstructions.
result: For a near-group ring of a specified type with an abelian group and odd parameters, categorification is possible only under a restrictive numerical condition.
conclusion: The work provides new purely algebraic obstructions and constrains possible categorifications of near-group fusion rings.

title: The Inverse Mean First-Passage Time Problem
authors: Tommer D. Keidar, Shlomi Reuveni, Igor M. Sokolov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the mean first-passage time [MATH] for an overdamped particle in a one-dimensional potential landscape, and address the problem inverse to the textbook one: Given [MATH] as a function of starting distance, we look for a potential that realizes it. We derive the conditions on [MATH] under which such a potential exists. We show that while the power-law dependences [MATH] with [MATH] may be realized by monotonic potentials, any realizable [MATH] with superquadratic growth requires potential wells arbitrarily far from the target; [MATH] separates sliding from trapping-dominated motion regimes.
tldr: The paper solves an inverse problem for mean first-passage times of an overdamped particle in a one-dimensional potential, determining which passage-time functions can be realized by some potential landscape.
motivation: Mean first-passage time is a central quantity in stochastic transport and search processes, but the standard problem asks for the passage time given a potential. The authors instead ask what potentials are compatible with a prescribed mean first-passage time profile.
method: The authors analyze the mean first-passage time for overdamped one-dimensional diffusion in a potential and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a given distance-dependent mean first-passage time to be realizable by a potential.
result: They show that power-law dependences can be realized by monotonic potentials, while any realizable superquadratic growth requires potential wells arbitrarily far from the target, and identify a threshold separating sliding from trapping-dominated regimes.
conclusion: The work characterizes the inverse mean first-passage time problem and clarifies fundamental constraints on designing potential landscapes that produce desired stochastic arrival-time statistics.

title: Lattice Spin Systems Coupled To A Compact U(1) Gauge Field With Negative Gauge Coupling Favoring Frustration
authors: Ettore Vicari Claudio Bonati
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the phase diagram and nature of the phase transitions of three-dimensional compact lattice Abelian Higgs models with negative gauge coupling. These models describe multicomponent complex scalar fields coupled to a compact U(1) gauge field. Negative gauge coupling favors frustrated plaquette configurations, competing with the tendency of the matter ferromagnetic-like interaction to suppress frustration. Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling analyses of models with one- and two-component scalar fields of unit charge reveal a substantially richer phase structure than at nonnegative gauge coupling. For two components, the O(3) transition line associated with gauge-invariant bilinear ordering extends into the negative-coupling region, and turns into a first-order transition line with decreasing [MATH], toward the fully-frustrated [MATH] limit. An analogous first-order transition line is also found for the one-component scalar matter with negative gauge coupling. Both one- and two-component models exhibit two additional continuous transition lines at sufficiently large matter coupling. Their energy-cumulant scaling is consistent with three-dimensional Ising and XY critical exponents, suggesting topological transitions in the [MATH] and XY gauge universality classes, respectively. These results uncover additional phases generated by the competition between matter ordering and dynamical gauge frustration, whose physical characterization remains an open question.
tldr: The paper uses Monte Carlo simulations to map the phase diagram of three-dimensional compact lattice Abelian Higgs models with negative gauge coupling, revealing frustration-induced phases and transitions.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how negative gauge coupling, which favors frustrated plaquette configurations, competes with matter ordering and enriches the phase structure of lattice Abelian Higgs models.
method: They perform Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling analyses for one- and two-component complex scalar fields of unit charge coupled to a compact U(1) gauge field.
result: They find a richer phase diagram than for nonnegative coupling, including first-order transition lines toward the fully frustrated limit and additional continuous transitions consistent with 3D Ising and XY critical exponents.
conclusion: The work uncovers phases emerging from competition between matter ordering and dynamical gauge frustration, but their physical characterization remains open.

title: Maximum Entropy Explanation For The Ubiquity Of Power-law Mechanical Responses
authors: Sverre Holm
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ubiquitous power-law relaxation emerges from complex mechanical systems with a vast number of interacting exponential responses. Here we demonstrate that power-law responses satisfy a maximum entropy criterion, regulating the individual contributions under partial knowledge. This leads to a prediction that frequency range of validity decreases with power-law exponent, a property which is confirmed for some biological materials. The close relation with the fractional standard linear solid also leads to an incorporation of the equally ubiquitous stretched exponential behavior.
tldr: The paper derives ubiquitous power-law mechanical relaxation from a maximum entropy criterion over distributed exponential responses.
motivation: Power-law relaxation appears across many complex mechanical and biological systems, but a unified thermodynamic-information explanation is lacking.
method: The author applies maximum entropy reasoning to regulate individual exponential contributions under partial knowledge and relates the result to fractional standard linear solid models and stretched exponential behavior.
result: The maximum entropy criterion predicts that the frequency range of validity decreases with the power-law exponent, a trend confirmed for some biological materials.
conclusion: Power-law mechanical responses can be understood as maximum entropy outcomes, linking fractional viscoelastic models with stretched exponential relaxation.

title: Hyperrigidity And Convexity In Two Variables
authors: Pawe{\l} Pietrzycki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend Brown's one-variable rigidity theorem to strictly convex functions of two variables under a regularity assumption. Let [MATH] be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let [MATH] be real-valued, strictly convex on [MATH], and of class [MATH] on a neighbourhood of [MATH]. We prove that the generating set [MATH] is hyperrigid in [MATH].
tldr: The paper extends Brown's one-variable hyperrigidity (rigidity) theorem to strictly convex functions of two variables under a smoothness assumption, showing that a certain generating set is hyperrigid in a C*-algebra.
motivation: Brown's rigidity theorem characterizes when a generating set of a C*-algebra is hyperrigid in the one-variable case; the author aims to extend this operator-system-theoretic result to functions of two variables.
method: Pure functional-analytic and operator-algebraic arguments: assuming the compact convex set is nonempty and the function is real-valued, strictly convex, and smooth on a neighbourhood, the proof establishes hyperrigidity of the associated generating set.
result: The generating set arising from a strictly convex two-variable function on a compact convex set is proven to be hyperrigid in the corresponding C*-algebra, generalizing the one-variable rigidity theorem.
conclusion: The work broadens the scope of hyperrigidity/rigidity results in operator systems theory, though it remains a purely mathematical contribution with no direct bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Generating Forbidden Words And Measures Of Maximal Entropy For Subshifts
authors: Xu Zhang Xinxing Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that if the entropy of generating forbidden words of a subshift over a finite alphabet is strictly smaller than its topological entropy, then the subshift has only finitely many ergodic measures of maximal entropy, each of which is Bernoulli up to a finite period, and admits a characteristic measure of maximal entropy. In particular, these conclusions hold when the entropy of minimal forbidden words is strictly smaller than the topological entropy, giving a negative answer to a question of Buzzi.
tldr: The paper studies subshifts over finite alphabets and proves that if the entropy of generating forbidden words is below the topological entropy, then the subshift has finitely many ergodic measures of maximal entropy, each Bernoulli up to finite period, and admits a characteristic measure of maximal entropy.
motivation: The work addresses a question of Buzzi concerning the structure of measures of maximal entropy under conditions on forbidden-word entropy, and aims to relate generating forbidden words to uniqueness/finiteness properties of maximal-entropy measures.
method: It uses symbolic dynamics and ergodic theory techniques, comparing the entropy of generating or minimal forbidden words with topological entropy to derive structural consequences for ergodic measures of maximal entropy.
result: Under the stated entropy gap condition, the subshift has only finitely many ergodic measures of maximal entropy, each is Bernoulli up to a finite period, and there exists a characteristic measure of maximal entropy; a negative answer to Buzzi's question is obtained.
conclusion: The paper establishes finiteness and Bernoulli-like structure of maximal-entropy measures for subshifts when forbidden-word entropy is strictly smaller than topological entropy, with implications for symbolic dynamics and ergodic theory.

title: The Askey-Wilson Function Is The Laplace Transform Of A Positive Measure
authors: Aaron Agulnick
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Askey-Wilson function [MATH] is a meromorphic continuation of the Askey-Wilson polynomials in their spectral variable off the lattice [MATH]. We show that the analytic part of the Askey-Wilson function [MATH] is the Laplace transform of a positive measure of total measure [MATH], under certain conditions on the parameters governing the function. We deduce log-convexity of this function, as well as positive-definiteness and an integral formula for a certain intertwining operator associated with the Askey-Wilson operator [MATH]. This offers a [MATH]-analogue of several results, in the trigonometric limit due to Sahi-McSwiggen, and in the rational (i.e. Dunkl) limit due to R\"osler.
tldr: The paper proves that the analytic part of the Askey-Wilson function is the Laplace transform of a positive measure of total mass one, yielding log-convexity, positive-definiteness, and an integral formula for the associated intertwining operator.
motivation: The Askey-Wilson function is a meromorphic continuation of the Askey-Wilson polynomials off the lattice, and the authors seek a q-analogue of positivity and integral representation results previously established in the trigonometric (Sahi–McSwiggen) and rational/Dunkl (Rösler) limits.
method: Analytic techniques in the theory of q-special functions: explicit analysis of the analytic part of the Askey-Wilson function and construction of a positive measure whose Laplace transform it is, under parameter conditions.
result: Under suitable parameter restrictions, the analytic part of the Askey-Wilson function is a Laplace transform of a positive measure of total measure one, from which log-convexity, positive-definiteness, and an integral formula for the intertwining operator of the Askey-Wilson operator follow.
conclusion: The work extends positivity and representation theorems for Askey-Wilson-type functions across the q, trigonometric, and rational/Dunkl hierarchy, contributing to the harmonic analysis of q-orthogonal polynomial families.

title: Initial-Trace Insufficiency And Entropy-Accounting Separation In Finite-Volume Coarse Graining
authors: Antonis Polemitis (UNIC Evolve, University Of Nicosia, Nicosia, Cyprus), Nicholas Christakis (institute For Advanced Modelling And Simulation, University Of Nicosia, Nicosia, Cyprus), Dimitris Drikakis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coarse finite-volume information does not automatically define an exact pathwise closure for the restricted evolution of a fine-grid realization. We study two one-step information boundaries that are distinct from recursive predictive memory. First, we show that parent averages together with complete initial parent-interface trace pairs are sufficient for one forward-Euler finite-volume transition with a deterministic two-state numerical flux, but they do not generally determine a completed second-order strong-stability-preserving Runge-Kutta, equivalently Heun, transition. An explicit scalar upwind collision shows that hidden interior data can affect later stage traces and hence the completed parent update, even when initial traces and parent averages agree. Second, we show that exact conservative one-step closure is not the same as entropy-accounting closure. A parent entropy balance obtained from a cellwise numerical entropy balance contains a subcell Jensen gap, a realized entropy-flux difference, and residual dissipation. For a declared Burgers-Rusanov conservative flux and a declared Rusanov-type numerical entropy flux, we construct a sign-indexed finite family in which all branches have identical parent averages, identical conservative interface registers, and identical next parent averages, while the entropy-interface register distinguishes every branch. Under the uniform branch law, the conservative channel leaves nonzero deterministic squared-error floors for both the raw entropy register and its cyclic divergence. The results give a concise finite-volume information-sufficiency test for multistage interface data and entropy-side accounting.
tldr: The paper studies information sufficiency and entropy-accounting closure in finite-volume coarse graining for numerical PDE evolution, not quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: It asks whether coarse finite-volume data can exactly close fine-grid evolution and whether conservative closure implies entropy-accounting closure.
method: The authors analyze one-step forward-Euler and Heun/SSP-RK transitions, constructing explicit scalar upwind and Burgers-Rusanov examples with hidden subcell data and sign-indexed branch families.
result: Parent averages plus initial interface traces suffice for one forward-Euler step but not generally for completed second-order multistage updates; entropy-interface registers can distinguish branches that share conservative parent data.
conclusion: The work provides finite-volume information-sufficiency tests and shows a separation between conservative one-step closure and entropy-accounting closure.

title: Optimal Communication For Distributed Sparse Histogram Aggregation
authors: Yijun Fan Fangwei Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Histogram estimation is a fundamental primitive in distributed data analysis, with applications in counting queries and federated learning. In many settings, the universe of categories is enormous, yet each user's data involves only a small subset, yielding sparse local histograms. This raises a natural question: To what extent can local sparsity reduce the communication needed to estimate the global histogram? We answer this question by characterizing the communication complexity of distributed sparse histogram estimation under prescribed [MATH] distortion and failure probability constraints. Our upper bound is achieved by a randomized covering scheme that optimizes how accurately each user represents its local histogram to reduce communication. By exploiting the distortion budget directly rather than imposing unbiasedness, the scheme achieves lower communication costs than standard unbiased sampling and hashing constructions. We establish the scheme's first-order optimality through a lower bound based on local support identification. The key step is to relate communication cost directly to the number of active coordinates revealed by each user's message, rather than to bound information about the aggregate via distance-based Fano's inequalities. This characterization further quantifies how the communication advantage of heterogeneous over homogeneous encoders varies across parameter regimes.
tldr: The paper characterizes the communication complexity of distributed sparse histogram estimation under prescribed distortion and failure probability, giving a randomized covering scheme with matching lower bound.
motivation: Distributed histogram estimation is a basic primitive in federated learning and counting queries, and local sparsity in the enormous category universe motivates asking how much communication it can save.
method: A randomized covering scheme exploits the distortion budget directly (rather than enforcing unbiasedness) to decide how accurately each user encodes its local histogram, with a lower bound built on local support identification rather than distance-based Fano inequalities.
result: The scheme beats standard unbiased sampling and hashing constructions and is shown to be first-order optimal; the analysis also quantifies when heterogeneous encoders outperform homogeneous ones across parameter regimes.
conclusion: Local sparsity yields a communication advantage characterized by relating cost to the number of revealed active coordinates, settling the communication complexity of the problem up to first order.

title: Non-asymptotic Sphere-Packing Bounds For Finite-Blocklength Scalar Gaussian Multiple-Access And Broadcast Channels
authors: Kaixuan Bao, Wei Xu, Xiaohu You
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates non-asymptotic achievable rate regions of Gaussian multiple-access channels (MACs) and broadcast channels (BCs) in the finite-blocklength regime. By employing a proposed volume-uniform random coding (VURC) codebook that distributes codewords uniformly within an [MATH]-dimensional power sphere, together with successive interference cancellation (SIC) decoding, we derive a closed-form achievability bound, a scheme-specific lower bound on the average error probability, and a fourth-order asymptotic characterization. The proposed SIC achievability bound admits a simple and analytically interpretable closed-form expression, enabling direct performance evaluation without iterative computation. The structure of the proposed SIC asymptotic bound offers a highly extensible framework, allowing advances in single-user finite-blocklength theory to be systematically incorporated into the multiuser setting. Futhermore, to characterize the performance benefit of joint decoding, we further derive numerical and closed-form achievability bounds for the two-user Gaussian MAC under joint nearest-neighbor (JNN) decoding. Numerical results illustrate the performance differences among the proposed SIC and JNN bounds and existing benchmarks.
tldr: The paper derives non-asymptotic sphere-packing achievability and converse-type bounds for finite-blocklength scalar Gaussian multiple-access and broadcast channels using a volume-uniform random coding scheme and SIC/JNN decoding.
