method: Process models informed by industry data were coupled with life cycle assessment and Monte Carlo simulation to compare polysulfone versus cellulose-based membranes per square meter produced, across multiple impact categories.
result: Polymer and bore solution preparation contribute 30-80% of impacts, and solvent-contaminated wastewater management is a second hotspot; cellulose membranes perform worse than polysulfone in at least 85% of simulations per impact category, while solvent recycling with reduced water demand (below ~36 L/m2) yields climate benefits.
conclusion: Bio-based substitution alone does not reduce environmental burden due to chemical-intensive cellulose modification, whereas solvent recycling combined with water-demand reduction offers a more promising pathway to lower the footprint of membrane manufacturing.

title: Naturalization Of Vinti's Intermediary Orbit---or How To Get Rid Of Small Divisors In Brouwer's Satellite Solution
authors: Martin Lara
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A naturalization, in the sense of Deprit, of Vinti's dynamical system makes the construction of a first order analytical satellite perturbation solution without critical divisors possible. The process gives hints on how to recast Brouwer's classical solution in a form that is free from small divisors too. The functionality of classical perturbation solutions is in this way extended to the close vicinity of the critical inclination. The new analytical solution bears terms that may grow unbounded, but their negative effects do not disclose in time intervals in which this kind of solution may be useful in practice.
tldr: The paper constructs a first-order analytical satellite perturbation solution free of critical (small) divisors by applying Deprit-style naturalization to Vinti's intermediary orbit, and shows how Brouwer's classical solution can be recast in the same divisor-free form.
motivation: Classical analytical satellite perturbation solutions break down near the critical inclination because of small divisors; the author seeks a reformulation that extends their validity to that regime.
method: A naturalization (in Deprit's sense) of Vinti's dynamical system is performed to build a first-order perturbation solution without critical divisors, with hints transferred to a recast of Brouwer's solution.
result: The resulting analytical solution remains functional in the close vicinity of the critical inclination, at the cost of terms that may grow unbounded but whose adverse effects stay negligible over practically useful time spans.
conclusion: Divisor-free perturbation solutions extend the practical applicability of classical satellite theories near the critical inclination, despite the presence of weakly growing secular-like terms.

title: Small Hankel Operators On Weighted Besov Spaces
authors: Kai Wang Chen Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize bounded small Hankel operators from [MATH] to [MATH] on the polydisc for [MATH], under explicit conditions relating the kernel parameter to the weight. When [MATH], boundedness is equivalent to a weighted Besov condition on the symbol; when [MATH], it is equivalent to a weighted supremum condition on a shifted radial derivative. In particular, the diagonal case is characterized by the product Bloch space. The proof combines weighted Bergman duality and atomic factorization with local kernel estimates and randomized atomic tests.
tldr: The paper characterizes boundedness of small Hankel operators acting on weighted Besov spaces over the polydisc, in terms of weighted Besov and Bloch-type conditions on the symbol.
motivation: Boundedness criteria for Hankel operators on Bergman-type spaces on the polydisc are a classical problem in complex analysis of several variables; the weighted Besov setting has remained uncharacterized for general kernel parameters.
method: The proofs combine weighted Bergman space duality, atomic factorization of Besov spaces, local estimates on the reproducing kernel, and randomized atomic testing arguments.
result: Boundedness is shown to be equivalent to a weighted Besov condition on the symbol when the kernel parameter is below a threshold, and to a weighted supremum condition on a shifted radial derivative above it, with the diagonal case characterized by a product Bloch space.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of bounded small Hankel operators between weighted Besov spaces on the polydisc, unifying and extending earlier Bergman-space results.

title: Fixed-grid Schemes For Fractional Moving-boundary Problems
authors: Conrard Giresse Tetsassi Feugmo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Landau transformation xi = x/s(t) is the usual way to hold a moving boundary in place. It fails for fractional time derivatives because they have no chain rule: the transformed operator gains a nonlocal integral with a closed form only for self-similar fronts. We develop a sharp-interface finite-difference scheme for the conservation-consistent memory-flux fractional Stefan problem on a fixed grid, storing the memory limit h(x) = s^-1(x) as the time each node melts. The front is advanced using an integrated energy balance, with the singular source timed to the sub-step crossing instant. Against a known self-similar solution, the front constant is accurate to 0.02 to 0.11%, whereas competing formulations differ by 17 to 27% at alpha = 0.6. A remaining positivity violation follows from dt/t0 ~ s0^(1 - 2/alpha) and disappears on a front-locked time grid. We also derive two exact solutions with non-power-law fronts: a source-dominated solution and a Mittag-Leffler traveling wave, and verify the scheme against both. Neural-network solvers for moving boundaries are often trained in normalized coordinates; for alpha < 1, this silently changes the problem, while the change vanishes at alpha = 1, where checks are commonly performed. In the classical limit, our scheme is more accurate in 12 ms than a reimplemented moving-boundary network in 177 s.
tldr: The paper develops a sharp-interface finite-difference scheme on fixed grids for fractional-time Stefan problems with moving boundaries, avoiding the Landau transformation that fails without a chain rule for fractional derivatives.
motivation: Standard moving-boundary coordinate transformations break down for fractional time derivatives because no chain rule exists, leaving a nonlocal integral term with closed form only for self-similar fronts; a robust fixed-grid method is therefore needed.
method: The authors store the melting-time memory limit h(x) = s^-1(x), advance the front via an integrated energy balance with a singular source timed to the sub-step crossing instant, and derive two exact non-power-law solutions (source-dominated and Mittag-Leffler traveling wave) for verification.
result: The front constant is accurate to 0.02–0.11% against the self-similar solution, versus 17–27% error for competing formulations at alpha = 0.6; a residual positivity violation traced to dt/t0 ~ s0^(1-2/alpha) vanishes on a front-locked time grid, and the scheme outperforms a moving-boundary neural network in both accuracy and runtime.
conclusion: The fixed-grid fractional Stefan scheme is accurate and efficient, and the paper warns that neural-network solvers trained in normalized coordinates silently alter the problem for alpha < 1, a pitfall masked by checks usually done at alpha = 1.

title: Descending Everest, Part Ii: Oracle Complexity Of Minimizing A Sum Of Convex $(L_0,L_1)$-Smooth Functions
authors: Mikhail Rudomanov, Ivan Fomin, Alexander V. Gasnikov, Fedor S. Stonyakin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimization of the average of [MATH] convex [MATH]-smooth functions: the Hessian norm of each function is bounded by an affine function of its gradient norm. We assume known upper bounds [MATH] on the distance from the starting point to a minimizer and [MATH] on the difference between the minimum of the average and the average of the infima of the components. We derive upper and lower bounds on the oracle complexity of reaching accuracy [MATH] in function value in expectation. Up to logarithmic factors, both bounds are of order [MATH]. The upper bound is attained by the proposed method YETI. The method combines ideas of accelerated proximal methods and variance reduction methods with a heuristic for choosing additional points. The number of oracle calls made by the heuristic is bounded, which preserves the upper bound on the total number of queries needed to reach the target accuracy. In the experiments, YETI is compared with first-order methods on synthetic problems and Poisson regression problems. We also examine the stopping criterion and the effect of the heuristic separately. The lower bound is obtained by an explicit construction of families of instances that are hard for any first-order method.
tldr: The paper derives matching (up to log factors) upper and lower oracle-complexity bounds for minimizing an average of convex (L0,L1)-smooth functions, achieved by a new method called YETI.
motivation: Optimization of functions with Hessian norms bounded by affine functions of gradient norms (generalized smoothness) lacks tight complexity characterizations, which matters for non-Euclidean and Poisson-regression-type problems.
method: The authors combine accelerated proximal methods with variance reduction and a bounded-query heuristic for selecting additional points (YETI), and prove a matching lower bound via an explicit construction of hard instance families for any first-order method.
result: Upper and lower bounds on oracle complexity to reach accuracy ε in function value in expectation coincide up to logarithmic factors, and experiments on synthetic and Poisson regression problems compare YETI against standard first-order methods.
conclusion: The work establishes near-optimal first-order complexity for (L0,L1)-smooth finite-sum convex minimization and characterizes the limits of any first-order approach.

title: Convergence Analysis Of TriCG And TriMR For Symmetric Quasi-definite Linear Systems
authors: Jia-Jun Fan Kui Du
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: TriCG and TriMR are two short-recurrence iterative methods introduced by Montoison and Orban [SIAM J.\ Sci.\ Comput., 43 (2021), pp.\ A2502--A2525] for solving symmetric quasi-definite linear systems. Extensive numerical experiments have demonstrated the efficiency of these two methods, but a systematic convergence analysis is still lacking. In this paper, we derive convergence bounds for the TriCG error norm and the TriMR residual norm. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results.
tldr: The paper derives convergence bounds for two short-recurrence Krylov-type iterative solvers, TriCG and TriMR, applied to symmetric quasi-definite linear systems.
motivation: TriCG and TriMR were shown empirically to be efficient solvers for symmetric quasi-definite systems, but no systematic convergence theory existed to explain or predict their behavior.
method: The authors derive theoretical convergence bounds for the TriCG error norm and the TriMR residual norm, then validate these bounds with numerical experiments.
result: Convergence bounds are established for both methods and are shown to be consistent with observed numerical behavior across test problems.
conclusion: The work supplies a missing convergence theory for TriCG and TriMR, giving practitioners theoretical grounding for these iterative solvers.

title: Quadratic Hubbard Trees, Automata, And Ray Connections
authors: Eduardo Ventilari Sodr\'e
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We describe an algorithm that, given a postcritically finite quadratic polynomial, outputs a finite state machine whose regular language is the set of external arguments for all points on the Hubbard tree, generalizing an example of Milnor. We do this by extracting orbit portraits from angled internal addresses, and constructing a suitable Markov partition of angle intervals. A main application is computing direct ray connections between Hubbard trees in matings of quadratic polynomials. We use this to understand ray connections in quadratic matings along veins of the Mandelbrot set, and prove that first ray connections between Hubbard trees are picked up at parabolic parameters or tips of veins.
tldr: An algorithm is presented that, for a postcritically finite quadratic polynomial, constructs a finite-state automaton whose regular language describes the external arguments of all points on the associated Hubbard tree.
motivation: Hubbard trees and ray connections encode the combinatorics of postcritically finite quadratic polynomials; a systematic, automaton-based method generalizes Milnor's example and enables computation of direct ray connections in matings.
method: Orbit portraits are extracted from angled internal addresses, a Markov partition of angle intervals is built, and from it a finite state machine is derived whose accepted language gives the external arguments on the Hubbard tree.
result: The construction yields computable ray connections between Hubbard trees in quadratic matings, and it is proved that first ray connections between Hubbard trees arise at parabolic parameters or at tips of veins of the Mandelbrot set.
conclusion: The automaton approach provides a concrete computational tool for complex dynamics and gives structural insight into ray connections along Mandelbrot set veins.

title: It Is Time For A New Deal For Mathematics
authors: Nestor Guillen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The AI labs' vision is based on extraction (of data, wealth, and political power). Mathematicians must oppose it, moving past personal reflections and towards reforming mathematics' social contract.
tldr: A commentary arguing that mathematicians should organize against AI labs' extractive vision by reforming mathematics' social contract.
motivation: The author contends that the AI industry's agenda is built on extraction of data, wealth, and political power, and that mathematicians must respond collectively rather than through individual reflection.
method: Opinion/position piece; no technical formalism, data analysis, or scientific methodology is employed.
result: The piece offers a call to action for the mathematics community to reshape its professional and social norms in opposition to AI-driven extraction.
conclusion: Mathematics as a discipline should adopt a new 'deal' governing its relationship with industry and society, moving beyond personal reflection to structural reform.

title: Limit Cycles Of Singular Algebraic Foliations On The Real Projective Plane
authors: Tianwei Gan, Hongjin He, Dongmei Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we consider cycles of singular algebraic foliations on the real projective plane. Our first result shows that there exists a limit cycle of singular algebraic foliations such that the limit cycle cannot be realized in any affine chart, that is, it fails to appear in any affine plane via the usual dehomogenization. On the other hand, under an appropriate convexity assumption, we verify that a cycle becomes fully visible, lying entirely in some affine chart. We then analyze the accumulation behavior of limit cycles of singular algebraic foliations on the real projective plane. Last we prove that algebraic foliations of degree at most two on the real projective plane have only finitely many limit cycles, and the maximum number of limit cycle is zero, one and at least six for algebraic foliations of degree zero, one and two on the real projective plane, respectively. This result extends Bamon's finiteness theorem for quadratic affine vector fields in [Publ. Math. IH\'ES, (64)1986, pp. 111--142].
tldr: The paper studies limit cycles of singular algebraic foliations on the real projective plane, proving visibility results, finiteness for quadratic foliations, and bounds on the number of limit cycles.
motivation: Extends classical finiteness results for limit cycles of polynomial vector fields (Bamon's theorem for quadratic affine vector fields) to the setting of singular algebraic foliations on the projective plane.
method: Geometric and topological analysis of foliations on RP^2, using dehomogenization/affine chart arguments, convexity assumptions, and accumulation analysis of limit cycles, together with degree-based case analysis.
result: Exhibits a limit cycle not realizable in any affine chart; shows that under convexity a cycle lies fully in some affine chart; proves degree-2 real projective foliations have finitely many limit cycles with maximum counts zero, one, and at least six for degrees zero, one, and two.
conclusion: The work generalizes Bamon's finiteness theorem to singular algebraic foliations on the real projective plane and establishes sharp-ish bounds on limit cycle counts by degree.

title: Star-shaped Periodic Solutions Of A System Of Delay Differential Equations: A Computer-assisted Proof
authors: Akitoshi Takayasu Shoya Motonaga
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we consider a planar system of nonlinear delay differential equations and prove the existence of the star-shaped periodic solutions conjectured by Hara (Nonlinear Analysis: Theory, Methods \& Applications, 30:4555--4563 (1997)) for seven parameter values. These solutions cannot be obtained by a direct application of the standard Fourier spectral method, since the corresponding linearized operator is degenerate. From numerical observations of the Fourier coefficients, we derive an ansatz that writes a star-shaped periodic solution as a periodic profile in a rotating frame. Restricting the profile to real Fourier coefficients, we show that the resonance between the delay and the period of the profile fixes the rotation frequency exactly. We then validate a zero of the resulting real system with the radii polynomial approach and interval arithmetic, with bounds that cover all Fourier modes. For each parameter value, we also determine the fundamental period and the winding number of the solution.
tldr: A computer-assisted proof establishes the existence of star-shaped periodic solutions for a planar system of nonlinear delay differential equations, confirming a conjecture by Hara for seven parameter values.
motivation: Hara conjectured the existence of star-shaped periodic solutions in a planar delay differential equation system, but these solutions are not accessible to standard Fourier spectral methods because the linearized operator is degenerate.
method: The authors use numerically observed Fourier coefficients to formulate an ansatz that expresses each star-shaped periodic solution as a periodic profile in a rotating frame. Restricting to real Fourier coefficients makes the resonance between delay and period fix the rotation frequency exactly, after which the authors validate a zero of the resulting real system using the radii polynomial approach with interval arithmetic.
result: Existence of the conjectured star-shaped periodic solutions is rigorously proven for seven parameter values, with bounds covering all Fourier modes; the fundamental period and winding number are determined for each case.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that computer-assisted rigorous numerics, combined with a well-chosen rotating-frame ansatz, can handle degenerate linearized operators that defeat standard spectral methods, thereby confirming Hara's conjecture in the given parameter regimes.

title: InterceptFuzz: Interception-based Stateful Fuzzing Of Single-Process Targets
authors: Ilja Siro\v{s}, Dave Singel\'ee, Bart Preneel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stateful protocol implementations are commonly fuzzed by tools that act as a network client and exchange messages with the target over sockets. Some wireless and IoT protocol stacks instead provide a single-process simulation platform, in which all nodes run in one binary and exchange packets in memory. Such simulations are deterministic and fast, which suits fuzzing, but offer no socket to which existing stateful fuzzers can attach. Meanwhile, fuzzing infrastructure such as Google's OSS-Fuzz supports only stateless engines. This paper presents InterceptFuzz, a middleware that enables stateful fuzzing of single-process targets on top of an unmodified stateless fuzzing engine. InterceptFuzz requires only a hook where the target passes packets between nodes. Through this hook, it records benign traffic and injects fuzzed packets. It organizes the observed packet sequences in a Prefix Tree. Each seed carries a State ID that selects a node of this tree, and InterceptFuzz deterministically replays the recorded prefix before delivering the mutated packet. The tree grows with newly discovered sequences, while redundant states are pruned to keep its growth in check. InterceptFuzz powered by AFL++ is evaluated on the Nexus test framework of OpenThread and on the LTE and Wi-Fi models of ns-3, against an interception-based adaptation of AFLNet and against Concat, an AFL++-based baseline that mutates a whole message sequence as one input. On OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, InterceptFuzz covers significantly more branches than both baselines. Seven previously unknown crash signatures were found in OpenThread. Concat, despite its simplicity, covers more branches than AFLNet in every campaign on OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, and on OpenThread it exposes the same crash signatures as InterceptFuzz, although some of them in fewer campaigns.
tldr: InterceptFuzz is a middleware that enables stateful fuzzing of single-process network simulation targets on top of unmodified stateless fuzzing engines by intercepting in-memory packet exchanges.
motivation: Wireless and IoT protocol stacks are often simulated as single binaries with in-memory packet passing, leaving no socket for existing stateful fuzzers to attach to, while popular infrastructure like OSS-Fuzz only supports stateless engines.
method: The tool requires a single hook where the target passes packets between nodes; it records benign traffic, organizes packet sequences in a prefix tree, assigns each seed a State ID selecting a tree node, and deterministically replays the recorded prefix before injecting a mutated packet, with pruning of redundant states.
result: InterceptFuzz built on AFL++ was evaluated on OpenThread's Nexus framework and ns-3 LTE/Wi-Fi models, covering significantly more branches than an interception-based AFLNet adaptation and a Concat baseline on OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, and discovering seven previously unknown crash signatures in OpenThread.
conclusion: The approach shows that stateful fuzzing of single-process simulation targets is feasible atop stateless fuzzing infrastructure, improving coverage and bug discovery for protocol stacks.

title: Revisiting Elliptic++ For Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction And Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
authors: Runlin Liang, Simon Trimborn, Noud van Giersbergen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from [MATH] under the original leaky evaluation to just [MATH] under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.
tldr: This paper identifies temporal information leakage in the Elliptic++ Bitcoin forensics benchmark and proposes a leakage-resistant feature reconstruction and evaluation pipeline.
motivation: Elliptic++ is widely used for Bitcoin forensic machine learning, but its positional train/test split and undocumented address-level feature definitions may allow future information leakage and inflate model performance.
method: The authors reverse-engineer the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features using public ledger data and recompute them with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at prediction time.
result: Under the original leaky evaluation, random forest achieves a strong illicit-class F1 score, but under the leakage-resistant pipeline its F1 drops sharply and it no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline.
conclusion: The authors provide exact feature definitions and executable code so future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.

title: Can Benign Skills Induce Misaligned Behavior In Llm Agents?
authors: Xuanye Zhang, Yongsen Zheng, Kaiyu Zhou, Bowen Shen, Haoran Ou, Zhuqin Xu, Tianwei Zhang, Kwok-Yan Lam
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills to plan tasks, invoke tools, recover from errors, and complete workflows without modifying model parameters. Although these skills are typically developed to enhance benign tasks, they may also make an agent more capable of executing procedures for harmful purposes. We study this risk, which we call skill-induced behavioral misalignment: adding benign skills may cause an agent to execute external actions that violate safety requirements. We first conduct a systematic study to validate the existence of this phenomenon. It compares agents with and without benign skills across five LLM backbones and three benchmarks under matched requests. On average, skill augmentation improves benign task accuracy by 10.3 percentage points (pp), but also increases unsafe action rate (UAR) by 10.3 pp. The regression also occurs with skills curated by experts. A paired trajectory analysis shows that 24 of 50 newly unsafe trajectories fail to complete the harmful objective, revealing violations that task completion alone would miss. We further disclose multiple factors and scenarios that could exacerbate this risk. (1) Evolving skills with benign feedback can amplify unsafe execution; (2) This regression is more pronounced when retrieved skills are matched to task and contain procedural guidance; (3) Distilling benign experience into reusable skills yield higher UAR compared with their source trajectories. (4) A guard that checks proposed tool actions before execution reduces violations while retaining gains on benign tasks. All these findings confirm the significance of skill-induced behavioral misalignment, and the urgent need for new mitigation solutions.
tldr: The paper identifies and empirically characterizes 'skill-induced behavioral misalignment', where adding benign reusable skills to LLM agents raises both task accuracy and unsafe action rates.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable, parameter-free skills built for benign purposes, but the authors argue these same skills may equip agents to carry out harmful procedures.
method: They compare agents with and without benign skills across five LLM backbones and three benchmarks under matched requests, plus paired trajectory analysis, skill-evolution and distillation studies, and a pre-execution tool-action guard.
result: Skill augmentation improves benign accuracy by 10.3 pp while raising the unsafe action rate by 10.3 pp, with 24 of 50 newly unsafe trajectories failing the harmful objective yet still violating safety requirements; risks grow with benign-feedback skill evolution, task-matched procedural skills, and distilled skills.
conclusion: Skill-induced misalignment is a significant and underappreciated safety risk for LLM agents, and simple pre-execution action guards partially mitigate it, motivating new mitigation approaches.

title: TxBench: A Benchmark Of Attack Transactions And Evidence-Backed Negatives On Seven Evm Chains
authors: Karim Ali Tamer Abdelaziz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers evaluate detectors of malicious smart-contract transactions on datasets that each paper assembles anew. Their positives come from incident trackers, whose citations mix attacks with setup steps and transactions that never ran, or from a detector's own output, which makes the evaluation circular; their negatives are ordinary transactions. A shared benchmark needs positives whose own execution shows the attack and negatives that use the attacks' mechanisms, with no detector deciding either label. We present TxBench, a benchmark of attack transactions and evidence-backed negatives on seven EVM chains, with the five-step pipeline that builds it. The pipeline collects every transaction that BlockSec's incident library or the EVM Hack Registry cites, maps its weakness to OWASP's SCWE taxonomy, and rebuilds its execution from free data sources. A cited transaction qualifies as a valid TxBench attack only if it extracts value from others during execution, is consistent with all verified source claims, and is independently linked to the reported incident by corroborating evidence. Negative examples are sampled from each chain's traffic near the attacks and retained only when positive evidence confirms their legitimacy. Of 1,850 cited transactions, TxBench accepts 1,012 attacks from 602 incidents, worth USD 868.1 million: 846 contract exploits and 166 key compromises. A blind review under rules fixed in advance confirms 98 of 100 sampled attacks (97.7% weighted) and all 100 sampled negatives. As baselines, four zero-shot LLMs reading anonymized traces are precise but find at most 0.43 of the attacks and no key compromise, leaving ample room for better detectors.
tldr: TxBench is a curated benchmark of 1,012 verified smart-contract attack transactions (and evidence-backed negatives) drawn from seven EVM chains, built via a five-step evidence-corroboration pipeline.
motivation: Existing smart-contract attack detectors are evaluated on ad hoc, self-assembled datasets whose positives are noisy incident citations and whose negatives are ordinary traffic, producing circular and non-comparable evaluations.
method: The pipeline collects transactions cited by BlockSec's incident library and the EVM Hack Registry, maps weaknesses to the OWASP SCWE taxonomy, replays execution from free data sources, and admits a positive only if it extracts value, matches verified source claims, and is independently corroborated; negatives are sampled near attacks and kept only with positive legitimacy evidence.
result: Of 1,850 cited transactions, 1,012 attacks from 602 incidents (USD 868.1M, 846 contract exploits and 166 key compromises) are accepted; blind review confirms 98/100 sampled attacks and 100/100 negatives, while four zero-shot LLMs find at most 0.43 of attacks and no key compromises.
conclusion: TxBench supplies a detector-independent, evidence-backed evaluation standard for blockchain attack detection and shows current LLM baselines are far from adequate.

title: On The Complexity Of Exact Autobidding Equilibria
authors: Yiyang Huang, Zhengyang Liu, Yonglei Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autobidding equilibria link advertisers' value multipliers or participation probabilities through aggregate budget and return-on-investment (ROI) constraints. We establish the exact computational complexity of finding these equilibria across several canonical settings: exact equilibrium computation is [MATH]-complete for second-price ROI pacing, budget- or ROI-constrained generalized second-price (GSP) sponsored shopping, and second-price throttling. Furthermore, approximating the equilibrium control vector in distance to a true equilibrium is [MATH]-complete when the target accuracy is provided as input.
tldr: The paper determines the exact computational complexity of computing autobidding equilibria in sponsored-search advertising auctions, showing several variants are complete for a complexity class (likely PPAD/CLS-type) even to approximate.
motivation: Autobidding systems with budget and ROI constraints are widely deployed in real ad auctions, but the computational difficulty of finding their equilibria was previously unresolved.
method: Complexity-theoretic reductions establishing completeness results for exact equilibrium computation under second-price ROI pacing, budget/ROI-constrained GSP sponsored shopping, and second-price throttling, plus hardness of approximation in distance to a true equilibrium.
result: Exact equilibrium computation is complete for the relevant class in all three canonical settings, and approximating the equilibrium control vector within a given accuracy is likewise hard.
conclusion: Computing autobidding equilibria is intractable in general, which informs the design of practical pacing algorithms and equilibrium-seeking mechanisms.

title: Beyond The Federer Paradox In Tennis
authors: Andr\'es Mart\'in, Johann H. Mart\'inez, Javier M. Buld\'u
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Roger Federer won about 80% of his professional matches with only 54% of the points. Hierarchical scoring amplifies small advantages on points into large advantages on matches, but also allows a player to win with fewer points than the opponent. Using Monte Carlo simulations and exact Markov chain calculations, we show that in tennis, badminton, volleyball and table tennis this amplification is set almost entirely by the number of points per match. We then let a player win ordinary points with probability p1 and crucial points, those closing a game, set or match, with probability p2. In every sport a narrow region of the (p1, p2) plane exists where a player wins most matches with fewer than half of the points, because crucial points carry more influence than their share of points. Of ATP matches played in 1991-2025, 4.7% were won with fewer points, 16% more than independent points predict (5% including the serve), a constant excess. Pressure performance measured in other seasons predicts match outcomes beyond the points won, and Fabio Fognini won 51% of his matches with 49% of the points, in what we call the Fognini paradox.
tldr: The paper analyzes hierarchical scoring in tennis, badminton, volleyball, and table tennis to explain how players can win matches despite winning fewer total points.
motivation: It aims to explain the Federer paradox and similar cases where match outcomes amplify small point-level advantages or allow wins with fewer points due to the greater weight of crucial points.
method: The authors use Monte Carlo simulations and exact Markov chain calculations, modeling ordinary and crucial-point win probabilities separately.
result: They find that amplification is set mainly by points per match, identify a narrow region where players win most matches with fewer than half the points, and report that 4.7% of ATP matches from 1991–2025 were won with fewer points.
conclusion: The work characterizes a scoring-induced paradox in racket and ball sports and shows that pressure performance can predict match outcomes beyond total points won.

title: Fractional Orbital Bombardment Systems
authors: Steve Fetter David Wright
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze Fractional Orbital Bombardment Systems (FOBS) as a means of delivering nuclear weapons by placing warheads into partial orbits around the Earth, and show that they do not represent a game-changing advance in technology or capability. We consider potential uses of such a weapon, including evading missile defenses and delivering attacks with short warning time. FOBS could underfly current exoatmospheric defenses, but the required payload reduction may not justify its use if other countermeasures are deemed effective. If a FOBS attack could be successfully disguised as a satellite launch, the warning time could be short enough to raise fears of a decapitating strike. The development of such a capability could lead countries to shorten decision-making timelines in a crisis, which would be destabilizing. The US can take steps to ensure that very-short-warning attacks would not succeed, thereby enhancing deterrence during a crisis.
tldr: An analysis of Fractional Orbital Bombardment Systems (FOBS) concluding they offer no game-changing nuclear delivery capability, though very-short-warning disguised attacks could be destabilizing.
motivation: To assess whether placing warheads in partial Earth orbits constitutes a meaningful strategic or technological advance, particularly for evading missile defenses or enabling decapitating first strikes.
method: Policy and technical analysis of FOBS payload constraints, orbital mechanics, defense underflight geometry, and warning-time dynamics, framed around deterrence stability and crisis decision-making.
result: FOBS can underfly current exoatmospheric defenses but requires payload reductions that may not be worthwhile; if a launch could masquerade as a satellite launch, warning times could drop enough to raise decapitation fears and compress crisis decision timelines.
conclusion: FOBS is not a technological game-changer, but the US should harden and posture to defeat very-short-warning attacks in order to preserve deterrence and stability.

title: How Does One Cut A 30-60-90 Triangle?
authors: Ed Pegg Jr, Brian Trease, Andrew Hudson, D. S. Mcneil
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We enumerate dissections of a 30-60-90 triangle into smaller triangles similar to itself, counting unlabeled arrangements up to similarity and reflection. There are 18 four-piece, 121 five-piece, and 844 six-piece arrangements, corresponding to 11, 47, and 235 distinct multisets of piece areas. We present illustrated catalogs organized by these area multisets and distinguish layouts obtained by subdivision and local rotations or reflections from independent layouts. A separately implemented computational search reproduces every arrangement up to nine pieces, finding 460404 arrangements. Counts through nine pieces for five other classes of triangles are included for comparison.
tldr: The paper enumerates combinatorial dissections of a 30-60-90 triangle into smaller similar triangles, cataloging arrangements up to similarity and reflection for up to nine pieces.
motivation: The authors aim to systematically classify 'reptile'-style self-similar dissections of a specific right triangle, extending enumeration results to previously unexplored piece counts and comparing against other triangle classes.
method: An exhaustive computational enumeration is performed, counting unlabeled arrangements modulo similarity and reflection, grouping them by piece-area multisets and distinguishing subdivided layouts from independent ones; a separate search cross-validates results up to nine pieces.
result: They find 18 four-piece, 121 five-piece, and 844 six-piece arrangements (11, 47, 235 distinct area multisets), with the independent search confirming all arrangements up to nine pieces, totaling 460,404, plus comparative counts for five other triangle classes.
conclusion: The work provides illustrated catalogs and a reproducible enumeration methodology for triangle dissections, offering a reference for combinatorial geometry of self-similar tilings.

title: Large Deviation Of Preimages Of Points Under The Dynamics Of A Holomorphic Correspondence
authors: Shrihari Sridharan Bharath Krishna Seshadri
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Our main objective in this paper is to prove a large deviation result for the distribution of preimages of a point under the iteration of a holomorphic correspondence with respect to the unique equilibrium state associated to a H\"{o}lder continuous potential defined on the support of the Dinh-Sibony measure of the correspondence. As a consequence, we obtain a convergence result which generalises the result on equidistribution of preimages by Dinh and Sibony. We also study a situation where the Dinh-Sibony measure happens to be the unique measure of maximal entropy for an appropriate holomorphic correspondence and also record some comments that connect this work with some recent works in the literature.
tldr: Proves a large deviation principle for the distribution of preimages of a point under iterated holomorphic correspondences, relative to the equilibrium state of a Hölder potential on the support of the Dinh–Sibony measure.
motivation: Equidistribution of preimages (Dinh–Sibony) describes the typical asymptotic behaviour; this work quantifies the atypical fluctuations of that distribution at the level of large deviations.
method: Tools from pluripotential theory and ergodic theory of holomorphic correspondences: equilibrium (Dinh–Sibony) measures, Hölder continuous potentials, and a large deviation principle for the preimage-counting measures.
result: A large deviation principle is established, yielding as a corollary a convergence result that generalizes the Dinh–Sibony equidistribution theorem; the case where the Dinh–Sibony measure is the unique measure of maximal entropy is also examined.
conclusion: The results extend the classical equidistribution picture for holomorphic correspondences to a refined large-deviation description, with connections noted to related recent literature.

title: Variance-Reduced Stochastic Quasi-Newton Sqcqp Method For Nonlinear Programming Problems
authors: Md Abu Talhamainuddin Ansary Gopal Tiwari
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a variance-reduced stochastic quasi-Newton sequential quadratic constrained quadratic programming method (VR-QN-SQCQP) for finite-sum nonlinear optimization with equality and inequality constraints. Exact nonlinear-constraint Hessians are replaced entirely by safeguarded symmetric rank-one (SR1) curvature models built from first-order constraint gradients, while PAGE estimates the objective gradient and an exact \(L_1\) merit function provides globalization. Under explicit regularity, boundedness, relative QCQP-accuracy, and step-length assumptions, the analysis establishes almost-sure subsequential convergence to Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) points and, under stronger uniform step-length and error-control conditions, an expected \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) outer-iteration bound for the squared KKT residual. A conditional local stability result also compares learned-curvature directions with their exact-Hessian counterparts. Numerical experiments compare VR-QN-SQCQP against Exact-SQCQP-PAGE on Sparse PCA using 253,680 CDC BRFSS 2015 observations and on a dense nonlinear benchmark. Over ten seeds, both methods converge in all Sparse PCA runs, while on the dense benchmark the proposed method converges in 10/10 runs versus 9/10 for the exact-Hessian variant. The proposed method performs zero exact constraint-Hessian evaluations and reduces median curvature-construction time on the dense benchmark from 0.1230 s to 0.0111 s. Overall runtime benefits remain problem-dependent.
tldr: The paper proposes a variance-reduced stochastic quasi-Newton method for constrained nonlinear optimization and analyzes its convergence and numerical performance.
motivation: The authors aim to avoid expensive exact constraint-Hessian evaluations in stochastic sequential quadratic constrained quadratic programming while retaining convergence guarantees.
method: They replace exact nonlinear-constraint Hessians with safeguarded SR1 curvature models, use PAGE gradient estimation, and globalize with an exact L1 merit function.
result: The method achieves almost-sure subsequential convergence to KKT points and an expected O(epsilon^-2) outer-iteration bound, with numerical experiments showing reduced curvature-construction time on a dense benchmark.
conclusion: VR-QN-SQCQP is a practical stochastic optimization algorithm for finite-sum constrained problems, but runtime benefits remain problem-dependent.

title: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision
authors: Nitin Aravind Birur, Divyanshu Kumar, Sahil Agarwal, Prashanth Harshangi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Restricting what a model can say is often mistaken for restricting an attacker's influence over its decision. An attacker can add text to the evidence and steer the model toward a wrong answer that still belongs to the allowed set. We evaluate seven decision models spanning hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). We present Slot Attack, a black-box attack designed for decision models that appends text assembled from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-selected incorrect option. The method relies solely on returned label probabilities, achieves success rates of 32--99\% on initially correct decisions, and identifies the effective component combinations with a median of 17--72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal this vulnerability. Models with near-identical accuracy on the sampled tasks differ by about 20\%age points in attack success. We demonstrate that an attacker can force not just one wrong answer but every available one: on about 20\% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77\% for gpt-6-luna and 98\% for GLiNER2.5; a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out. A fixed answer set constrains a decision's form, not its source; robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.
tldr: The paper introduces Slot Attack, a black-box adversarial attack that appends component-assembled text to evidence to steer decision models toward attacker-selected incorrect labels within an allowed answer set.
motivation: Restricting a model's allowed outputs is often assumed to limit attacker influence, but attackers may still manipulate the model's decision among permitted answers. The authors test whether output constraints provide real robustness.
method: They evaluate seven decision models, including hosted APIs, open-weight models, and an encoder, on 16 tasks from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples. Slot Attack uses only returned label probabilities and appends text built from named components to steer predictions.
result: Slot Attack achieves 32–99% success on initially correct decisions with a median of 17–72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal the vulnerability, and models with near-identical accuracy differ by about 20 percentage points in attack success.
conclusion: A fixed answer set constrains only the form of a decision, not its source. Robustness must be measured per model, per task, and per version rather than inferred from output format or confidence thresholds.

title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations For Agent Skills
authors: Kuiyi Gao, Xue Liu, Bowei He
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.
tldr: RuntimeTickets is a runtime protocol for auditing and enforcing security obligations of third-party Agent Skills by linking LLM-proposed obligations to deterministic checks at network egress.
motivation: Third-party Agent Skills can conceal data exposure or output manipulation within legitimate workflows, and existing descriptions, tool permissions, or scanners cannot reliably determine whether execution satisfies user security requirements.
method: The authors derive a risk model from malicious-Skill datasets, generate adversarial-benign Skill pairs, and use an LLM to propose source-grounded security obligations whose tickets restrict host approvals and drive deterministic runtime checks and monitoring.
result: Evaluated at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks, RuntimeTickets achieved 0.0% overlook and 0.0% overkill rates, outperforming production Skill scanners and runtime baselines such as an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard.
conclusion: RuntimeTickets ties approved security requirements to verifiable execution evidence and provides a foundation for safe, auditable deployment of third-party Agent Skills.

title: The Native Menace: Host-to-Browser Cross-Boundary Attacks Via Native Messaging
authors: Jyotirmay Chauhan, Rownak Islam, Jason Polakis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern browsers are complex software platforms that users can customize through browser extensions to further expand their functionality. Extensions derive their functionality from privileged browser APIs that expose powerful capabilities. Prior work has extensively studied how malicious webpages or extensions can target those capabilities. However, prior research has overlooked the NativeMessaging API, which allows extensions to create a communication channel that bridges the gap between web content rendered in the browser and native apps running on the user's machine. This API enables workflows that cross the browser's boundary to perform critical operations (e.g., digital signing) or exchange sensitive data (e.g., credentials). In this paper, we conduct the first, to our knowledge, empirical security analysis of NativeMessaging, and present a novel attack that allows a non-privileged malicious native app to misuse browsers' native messaging capabilities to stealthily intercept sensitive communications or launch confused deputy attacks against other native apps. To demonstrate the significant risk introduced by native messaging, we present a series of concrete attacks against popular and critical apps (e.g., 1Password, the European Union's eID system, Google Drive), whose browser extensions have more than 532 million cumulative downloads. Our attacks have severe ramifications, including full password vault leakage, and arbitrary document signing in governmental workflows. Fundamentally, these attacks are possible due to native messaging being built on top of an untrusted communication channel without providing a root of trust or enforcing some form of client attestation. Accordingly, we propose a straightforward mitigation technique of message encryption with out-of-band secret sharing, to prevent our attacks.
tldr: The paper presents an empirical security analysis of the browser NativeMessaging API and demonstrates host-to-browser cross-boundary attacks against popular native apps and their extensions.
motivation: Prior work has studied malicious webpages and extensions, but NativeMessaging as a bridge between browser content and native apps has been overlooked despite enabling sensitive workflows such as credential exchange and digital signing.
method: The authors perform the first empirical security analysis of NativeMessaging and construct concrete attacks that let a non-privileged malicious native app intercept sensitive communications or launch confused-deputy attacks against other native apps.
result: They demonstrate attacks against high-impact apps including 1Password, the EU eID system, and Google Drive, whose extensions have over 532 million cumulative downloads, achieving effects such as password vault leakage and arbitrary document signing.
conclusion: The root cause is NativeMessaging's reliance on an untrusted communication channel without a root of trust or client attestation; the authors propose message encryption with out-of-band secret sharing as a mitigation.

title: Right Tool, Wrong Parameters: Defending Llm Agents Against Parameter Poisoning
authors: Yao Wang, Zehua Ma, Weiming Zhang, Han Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.04673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) poses a critical threat to LLM agents. Existing defenses largely focus on whether an injection induces a new tool invocation or unintended action. In this paper, we study a different attack surface, parameter poisoning, where the attacker preserves the intended action but manipulates one or more tool arguments, such as a recipient or other task-critical value. Such attacks are difficult to detect because no new action is introduced, while parameter changes themselves are often legitimate parts of the user's request. Our key insight is that the legitimacy of a parameter change should be determined by the trust of the information flow that produces it under the user query. The query induces a task-specific trust hierarchy over available information fields: some are trusted to determine particular parameters, while others should have little or no influence. Based on this insight, we propose AuthorityFlow, a three-stage parameter-level defense. First, it interprets the user query to construct a task-specific trust hierarchy over the information fields available to the agent. Second, for each tool argument, it traces the information flow that produces its current value and attributes the value to its supporting field. Finally, it accepts the value only when that field is trusted to determine the parameter under the current task, allowing high-trust changes while flagging low-trust influence as potential parameter poisoning. We further introduce FactAuthBench for evaluating parameter poisoning in LLM agents. Without defense, the attack success rate reaches 93.06%. AuthorityFlow reduces it to 9.03%, while retaining 82.64% benign task utility compared with 90.28% without defense. Our results show that effective IPI defense requires reasoning not only about what action an agent takes, but also about which information is trusted to determine its parameters.
tldr: The paper proposes AuthorityFlow, a parameter-level defense against indirect prompt injection attacks that poison tool arguments in LLM agents.
motivation: Existing IPI defenses focus on detecting new or unintended tool actions, leaving parameter poisoning—where the action stays the same but arguments are manipulated—largely unaddressed.
method: AuthorityFlow builds a task-specific trust hierarchy from the user query, traces each tool argument's information flow to its supporting field, and accepts the argument only when that field is trusted for the parameter.
result: Without defense, the attack success rate is 93.06%; AuthorityFlow reduces it to 9.03% while retaining 82.64% benign task utility compared with 90.28% without defense.
conclusion: Effective IPI defense requires reasoning about which information fields are trusted to determine tool parameters, not only about the agent's chosen action.

title: Exact Penalty Methods With Adaptive Discretization For Nonsmooth Semi-infinite Optimization
authors: Riccardo Tomassini Giancarlo Bigi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper considers a nonsmooth semi-infinite optimization problem in which the constraints are reformulated through a value function. Stationary points of the cutting surface approximations are studied, showing that stationarity is preserved in the limit under boundedness of the associated sequence of multipliers. Building on these results, an algorithm that combines the cutting surface approximations with a penalty scheme is devised, together with some proximal variants. An exact penalty result is established under suitable global conditions, and numerical results are reported to compare the methods with existing exact penalty and cutting surface algorithms.
tldr: The paper develops exact penalty methods with adaptive discretization for nonsmooth semi-infinite optimization via cutting surface approximations.
motivation: Semi-infinite optimization with nonsmooth constraints is challenging because standard finite-dimensional algorithms do not directly apply, and one needs reliable stationarity and penalty frameworks.
method: The authors reformulate constraints through a value function, study cutting surface approximations and their stationary points, and combine them with penalty and proximal schemes.
result: They establish stationarity preservation in the limit under bounded multipliers, prove an exact penalty result under global conditions, and report numerical comparisons with existing exact penalty and cutting surface methods.
conclusion: The proposed approach provides a practical and theoretically grounded framework for nonsmooth semi-infinite optimization, though it is outside quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis Of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
authors: Emmanuela Andam, Emanuel S. Grant, Naima Kaabouch
abstract: ArXiv:2611.03774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most malware detection research focuses on identifying whether a file is malicious before it executes. Far less attention goes to what happens after infection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behavior across 37 families, grounded in dynamic sandbox execution using CAPEv2. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships, preserving relational structure that flat feature vectors discard. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families, and a per-family behavioral fingerprint analysis characterizes post-infection activity across registry, network, process, and API dimensions. An LLM explanation layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed behavioral evidence. The full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan at [URL].
tldr: This paper empirically analyzes post-infection malware behavior across 37 families using dynamic sandbox traces modeled as heterogeneous graphs.
motivation: Malware detection research focuses mainly on pre-execution classification, leaving post-infection behavior comparatively understudied.
method: The authors execute malware samples in CAPEv2, represent behavioral traces as heterogeneous graphs with typed nodes and edges, and train voting ensemble classifiers on graph-derived structural features.
result: The graph-based ensemble achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 MCC points, and distinguishes 24 malware families while generating MITRE ATT&CK-mapped LLM explanations.
conclusion: Relational graph modeling improves post-infection malware behavior analysis and supports analyst-readable reporting, but the work is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
